passages.title: End-of-Life Care Jurisprudence
passages.text: The Supreme Court's recent intervention in cases involving prolonged incapacitation has intensified constitutional debates on medical autonomy, with the Bench directing premier medical institutions to formulate palliative care protocols while invoking fundamental rights protections established in the 2018 Common Cause judgment. The Court emphasized that withdrawal of life support must preserve patient dignity through robust pain management, urging legislative action to prevent socio-economic biases from influencing end-of-life decisions. This judicial trajectory aligns with global precedents where jurisdictions like the Termination of Life on Request and Assisted Suicide Act in 2002—and Belgium have formalized regulatory frameworks for physician-assisted dying, while Switzerland permits assisted suicide without active euthanasia authorization. The Union Ministry's draft guidelines on withdrawal of life support in terminally ill patients, currently under stakeholder consultation, attempt to operationalize these constitutional principles through procedural safeguards including mandatory medical board assessments and living will registries. Critics argue that absent comprehensive legislation, patients remain vulnerable to arbitrary determinations, while proponents contend that the evolving jurisprudence recognizes the intrinsic connection between dignity and autonomy under the right to life protections. The Court's insistence on institutionalized palliative care rather than ad-hoc determinations reflects broader anxieties about medical ethics in resource-constrained environments, where familial and financial pressures may compromise patient welfare.

passages.title: Removal of CEC
passages.text: Constitutional provisions safeguarding the independence of electoral oversight bodies have drawn renewed parliamentary attention, with opposition mobilization seeking to initiate formal removal proceedings against current officeholders through mechanisms requiring rigorous evidentiary standards equivalent to those applied to judicial removals. Article 324's framework ensures that electoral commissioners can only be displaced through address-based proceedings in either legislative chamber, with threshold requirements of fifty members in the upper house or one hundred in the lower house, thereby insulating the institution from executive caprice. This procedural architecture mirrors the removal mechanisms for superior court judges under Article 124, reflecting the constitutional vision of electoral integrity as foundational to democratic legitimacy. Historical precedents reveal sporadic attempts to initiate such proceedings, though none have culminated in successful removal, underscoring the high evidentiary burden of proving misbehavior or incapacity. The current controversy involves allegations of electoral management irregularities in subnational jurisdictions, with opposition parties gathering signatures to formalize impeachment-style motions. Constitutional scholars emphasize that such procedural safeguards, while protecting institutional autonomy, also risk creating accountability gaps when commissioners face credible allegations of partisan bias. The debate illuminates persistent tensions between independence and accountability in electoral governance, with proposals for reform ranging from fixed tenure modifications to enhanced transparency in decision-making processes.

passages.title: Artificial Intelligence and Linguistic Sovereignty
passages.text:
The confluence of technological nationalism and linguistic preservation has manifested through high-profile deliberations at the national capital's premier convention complex, where global stakeholders converged to examine artificial intelligence applications spanning citizen welfare, environmental sustainability, and economic advancement. The gathering emphasized indigenous language technologies, including platforms documenting oral traditions of tribal communities whose dialects face extinction pressures from dominant regional languages, and real-time translation systems bridging vernacular communication barriers. These initiatives align with broader digital governance frameworks seeking to democratize access to emerging technologies while preserving cultural heritage. The computational infrastructure supporting these applications—drawing conceptual foundations from the 1956 Dartmouth Conference that formalized artificial intelligence as a disciplinary field—

enables speech-to-text conversion across diverse linguistic registers, from endangered tribal tongues to major regional languages. Critical perspectives highlight the digital divide risks, noting that marginalized communities may lack infrastructure access despite technological availability, while proponents contend that AI-enabled preservation can reverse linguistic attrition through corpus building and digital archiving. The intersection of language technology with healthcare and environmental applications—ranging from AI-assisted diagnostics to climate modeling—demonstrates the integrative vision of inclusive innovation, though implementation challenges regarding data privacy, algorithmic bias, and digital literacy remain unresolved.

passages.title: Digital Governance
passages.text:
India's digital governance framework has undergone a structural transformation between 2023 and 2026, anchored by two legislative pillars: the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDPA) and the IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026, both administered by MeitY. The constitutional foundation traces to Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), where a nine-judge bench held the Right to Privacy to be a fundamental right under Article 21, catalysing India's decade-long journey toward a comprehensive data protection law. Parliament enacted the DPDPA on 11 August 2023, with rules finalised on 13 November 2025, introducing key concepts of Data Fiduciaries and Data Principals, with a maximum penalty of ₹250 crore for violations. Full compliance obligations activate by May 2027.

The IT Amendment Rules, notified on 10 February 2026, introduced mandatory AI-content watermarking, platform traceability obligations, and alignment with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, replacing IPC references. Safe harbour protection under Section 79 of the IT Act now depends strictly on compliance with these obligations.

India now stands alongside the EU's GDPR and Brazil's LGPD as a jurisdiction with a comprehensive, rights- based digital governance architecture.

passages.title: Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0
passages.text:
The Cabinet’s decision to extend the Jal Jeevan Mission with a substantially enhanced financial outlay reflects the government’s continued focus on rural drinking water security as a cornerstone of inclusive development. Initially launched to provide tap connections to every rural household, the programme has achieved significant coverage, transforming the lives of millions of women who previously spent hours daily fetching water. Studies by various research institutions have quantified its positive impact on health outcomes, women’s economic participation, and child mortality rates.

The restructured approach under JJM 2.0 emphasises not merely infrastructure creation but long-term service delivery, sustainability, and community ownership. The introduction of digital monitoring systems and unique identification for water supply schemes aims to improve transparency and accountability at the grassroots level. Annual community events are being promoted to foster collective responsibility towards maintenance and source sustainability.

However, challenges related to water quality, declining groundwater levels, and operation and maintenance of assets remain significant. Experts suggest that convergence with other rural development schemes and greater involvement of local self-government institutions will be crucial for long-term success. As India moves towards its 2047 vision, ensuring reliable and safe drinking water supply in rural areas represents both a developmental necessity and a constitutional obligation towards improving quality of life across the country.

passages.title: GST 2.0
passages.text:
Nearly a decade after its historic inception, India's indirect tax architecture underwent a transformative structural overhaul to address persistent compliance friction and classification anomalies. The legacy system, burdened by a complex multi-tiered rate structure, frequently resulted in inverted duty challenges, legal ambiguities, and delayed input tax credit reconciliations. Recognizing the imperative to foster a frictionless, globally competitive business environment, the federal fiscal forum initiated a comprehensive modernization mandate, colloquially termed the next-generation overhaul.

This modernized framework functions by fundamentally rationalizing the tariff architecture. The previous complex matrices have been collapsed into a simplified, dual-slab core applied to the vast majority of goods and services, explicitly eliminating the intermediate and peak standard rates of the past. To sustain revenue buoyancy, this core is complemented by a specialized, higher punitive bracket strictly reserved for luxury commodities and socially detrimental goods, replacing previous compensation cess mechanisms. Beyond rate simplification, the new regime operates through aggressive technological integration—featuring automated e-invoicing, accelerated algorithmic refunds, and fully operationalized centralized appellate tribunals. Ultimately, this paradigm shift transitions the regulatory focus from policing evasion to proactively facilitating systemic economic formalization and transparent consumption.

passages.title: Emergency
passages.text: The emergency provisions in the Indian Constitution, enshrined in Part XVIII (Articles 352 to 360), are fundamentally designed to safeguard the sovereignty, unity, integrity, and security of the nation. The framers of the Constitution recognized that extraordinary crises—such as war, external aggression, armed rebellion, or severe financial instability—demand swift and highly centralized responses. During normal times, India functions as a federal democracy, distributing power between the Centre and the states. However, declaring an emergency effectively transforms this federal structure into a unitary one without requiring formal constitutional amendments. This temporary mechanism is required to grant the Central government overriding executive and legislative powers, ensuring that the country can navigate grave national threats or the breakdown of constitutional machinery in specific states without being hindered by procedural delays or divided authority. To craft these crucial safeguards, the framers borrowed and adapted concepts from previous legislative frameworks. The primary structural foundation for the emergency provisions was directly taken from the Government of India Act, 1935. This colonial-era legislation contained specific sections granting the executive vast discretionary powers to assume centralized control during a failure of governance or internal disturbances. Furthermore, while the overarching emergency framework originates from the 1935 Act, a specific feature—the suspension of Fundamental Rights during an active emergency—was borrowed from the Weimar Constitution of Germany. By combining these historical precedents with strict parliamentary oversight, the Constitution ensures the state has the strength to survive existential crises.

passages.title: Export Preparedness Index
passages.text:
The landscape of India’s international trade is increasingly defined by sub-national performance, a trend highlighted by the periodic release of the Export Preparedness Index (EPI). As the nation seeks to integrate more deeply into global value chains, this analytical framework has emerged as a essential tool for assessing how individual states facilitate and contribute to national export expansion. By offering a structured evaluation of regional trade readiness, the index assists policymakers in identifying barriers to commerce and optimizing local logistical frameworks.

The methodology behind the index is comprehensive, focusing on several foundational pillars that determine a state's capacity to engage in international trade. These pillars are designed to capture the multifaceted nature of export-oriented growth, ranging from governance structures and infrastructure development to the broader commercial climate. To ensure depth, these core pillars are further broken down into a variety of sub-pillars and specific indicators, allowing for precise, data-driven comparisons between states regardless of their industrial maturity or geographic location.

To facilitate better benchmarking, the index organizes states into specific performance tiers, distinguishing between those at different stages of their export journey. This classification system helps prioritize interventions, encouraging states to improve their trade facilitation measures and policy frameworks. Ultimately, the publication of this index by India's national policy think tank serves as a strategic compass, fostering healthy competition among states and providing a clear roadmap for enhancing India's overall export competitiveness on the global stage.

passages.title: OPEC and OPEC+
passages.text:
The global energy landscape underwent a tectonic shift in May 2026 when a major Middle Eastern nation formally announced its departure from the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and the broader OPEC+ alliance, ending a 59-year tenure. This move, driven by the nation's desire for greater autonomy in its production and export policies, sent immediate tremors through global oil markets, challenging the long- standing influence of the world’s most significant energy cartel.

The country's exit occurred against a backdrop of escalating regional instability. In early 2026, the Strait of Hormuz—the world’s most critical maritime chokepoint for oil transport—faced severe blockades due to heightened geopolitical tensions, which temporarily throttled the exiting nation's capacity to maximize its newly uncapped production. This maritime vulnerability highlighted the complex risks inherent in regional energy dominance.

OPEC, founded in 1960 and permanently headquartered in Vienna, Austria, has long served as the primary arbiter of global oil prices. Traditionally, Saudi Arabia acts as the organization's de facto leader and "swing producer," adjusting output to stabilize market volatility. In 2016, the organization evolved into OPEC+, an expanded alliance that integrates original OPEC members with critical non-OPEC producers to coordinate production levels on a global scale. While nations like Algeria remain steadfast members of the original bloc, this recent withdrawal underscores the growing difficulty in maintaining consensus. As the energy transition accelerates and individual nations pursue divergent national interests, the departure of a key player challenges OPEC’s historic ability to dictate supply dynamics, marking an uncertain chapter for global energy governance.

passages.title: ELNINO
passages.text:
The El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is a periodic fluctuation in sea surface temperatures and the air pressure of the overlying atmosphere across the equatorial. At its core, the phenomenon represents a dramatic shift in the "Walker Circulation"—a massive atmospheric loop that normally drives air westward across the tropical Pacific. Under neutral conditions, strong trade winds push warm surface waters, creating a "warm pool" near Indonesia and Australia, while cooler, nutrient-rich water upwells along the coast of South America.

When this system enters an El Niño phase, the trade winds weaken, allowing the accumulated warm water to surge eastward. Meteorologists distinguish "Super" events by the intensity of this warming, typically measuring deviations in sea surface temperatures in specific Pacific zones. This thermal shift disrupts global climate patterns by altering jet streams and heat distribution.

The ENSO cycle is monitored using the Southern Oscillation Index (SOI), which serves as an atmospheric barometer. By tracking the pressure gradient between the western and eastern Pacific, scientists can quantify the strength of the trade winds. When the SOI displays sustained negative values, it signals that the normal pressure "seesaw" has tilted, marking the onset of the warmer phase. Conversely, La Niña occurs when the trade winds intensify, pulling unusually cold water to the surface in the eastern Pacific. This atmospheric coupling creates a feedback loop that influences rainfall distribution, cyclone frequency, and agricultural outcomes across the globe, with distinct and often opposing impacts on the South Asian monsoon cycle.

passages.title: Russia–Ukraine Dispute: Beyond the Battlefield
passages.text: The conflict between Russia and Ukraine, which escalated into a full-scale war in 2022, has reshaped the strategic landscape of Europe and significantly altered global diplomacy. Although the immediate military confrontation is recent, the dispute is rooted in decades of political disagreements over sovereignty, security, and competing visions of the post-Cold War order. Successive developments—including constitutional changes within Ukraine, competing security arrangements in Europe, and disagreements over territorial status—gradually deepened mistrust between the two neighbours. The conflict has extended far beyond conventional warfare. International courts have been approached to examine allegations of war crimes and violations of humanitarian law, while economic sanctions imposed by several Western countries have attempted to restrict financial transactions, technology transfers, and energy exports. Simultaneously, Russia has sought to deepen economic engagement with partners outside the Western alliance system, reshaping patterns of global trade and energy flows. Maritime geography has also assumed strategic importance. Control over access routes linking enclosed regional seas with the wider Black Sea has influenced military logistics, commercial navigation, and international legal disputes. Infrastructure built across these waters has further intensified disagreements regarding sovereignty and freedom of navigation. The crisis has also revived broader debates over the expansion of military alliances, collective security arrangements, and the limits of international law in responding to armed conflict. As diplomatic negotiations continue intermittently, the dispute remains a defining test of the contemporary international order and the effectiveness of multilateral institutions in addressing prolonged interstate conflicts.

passages.title: Constitutional Democracy and the Limits of Popular Will
passages.text: In a significant constitutional observation delivered recently, the Supreme Court reiterated that democratic governance cannot be reduced merely to the rule of the numerical majority. While elected governments derive legitimacy from the will of the people, the Court emphasized that constitutional democracies are founded upon principles that protect individual freedoms, institutional independence, and the rights of minorities irrespective of changing political preferences. According to the Court, public opinion, however overwhelming, cannot justify actions inconsistent with constitutional guarantees. The observations arose while the Court examined a challenge involving the relationship between governmental action and constitutional values. During the proceedings, the Bench highlighted that the Constitution establishes a framework in which every organ of the State is constrained by legal limitations, ensuring that political power remains accountable to constitutional norms rather than transient electoral mandates. Such limitations, the Court observed, preserve the balance between democratic governance and the rule of law. The judgment has renewed discussions on the distinction between electoral legitimacy and constitutional legitimacy. Constitutional experts note that while elections determine who governs, the Constitution determines how governance must be exercised. This distinction assumes particular significance in plural societies where competing social, religious, linguistic, and cultural identities coexist under a common constitutional framework. The observations also reinforce the continuing role of constitutional courts in reviewing legislative and executive action. Judicial review, separation of powers, and the protection of fundamental rights together function as institutional safeguards intended to prevent arbitrary exercise of authority while preserving democratic accountability within constitutional limits.

passages.title: Archaeology, Heritage and Judicial Adjudication
passages.text: A recent judicial proceeding concerning a historically significant monument in central India has once again highlighted. The Bhojshala–Kamal Maula complex at Dhar in Madhya Pradesh has long occupied a prominent place in debates concerning heritage, archaeology, and constitutional governance. The dispute centres on a centuries-old structure that has long been claimed by different communities, each relying on historical traditions, inscriptions, and documentary evidence to support competing assertions regarding its original character. During the proceedings, the High Court permitted a detailed archaeological survey to facilitate the collection of scientific evidence while emphasizing that questions relating to title and legal rights must ultimately be determined through due judicial process rather than public opinion or historical assertions alone. The case has renewed debates regarding the evidentiary value of archaeological findings in civil disputes involving places of worship and protected monuments. The controversy also illustrates the intersection of heritage conservation and constitutional rights. While archaeological agencies are entrusted with preserving monuments of national importance, courts are frequently required to balance conservation objectives with claims relating to religious practices, historical continuity, and public order. Legal experts have observed that archaeological evidence may assist courts in understanding the historical evolution of a site but does not, by itself, determine legal ownership or religious status. The proceedings have therefore attracted wider attention as an example of how constitutional institutions attempt to reconcile competing historical narratives within the framework of the rule of law, ensuring that disputes over cultural heritage are resolved through legal adjudication rather than political or majoritarian considerations.

passages.title: UNIFIED PAYMENTS INTERFACE (UPI) AT 10 YEARS
passages.text: Few technological innovations have transformed everyday life in India as profoundly as the Unified Payments Interface (UPI). Introduced during a period when digital transactions constituted only a small fraction of retail payments, the platform has evolved into one of the world's largest real-time payment ecosystems. Its remarkable expansion has been driven by interoperability, ease of use, low transaction costs, and widespread smartphone adoption. Over the past decade, digital payments have increasingly replaced cash transactions for individuals, businesses, and government services, reshaping India's financial landscape. The growth of the platform has also become an important instrument of financial inclusion. By enabling seamless transactions across banks through a common interface, the system has expanded access to formal financial services while encouraging innovation among fintech companies. Its architecture has supported the emergence of QR-code based payments, merchant digitisation, and new financial products that rely upon secure digital authentication. The platform's influence now extends beyond India's borders. Through partnerships with foreign governments and payment networks, digital payment acceptance has gradually expanded across several regions including Asia, Europe, and the Middle East. This internationalisation has complemented India's broader objective of promoting digital public infrastructure as a global public good while strengthening cross-border payment connectivity. The tenth anniversary of the platform has therefore been viewed not merely as a technological milestone but also as an illustration of how public digital infrastructure can reshape governance, commerce, and financial inclusion. Even as new challenges relating to cybersecurity, digital literacy, and payment resilience continue to emerge, policymakers increasingly view interoperable digital payment systems as an essential component of future economic growth and global financial cooperation.

India's transition towards cleaner and more sustainable sources of energy has increasingly focused on reducing dependence on imported crude oil while simultaneously supporting farmers through alternative markets for agricultural produce. One of the most significant initiatives in this direction has been the promotion of ethanol-blended petrol. Over the past decade, blending levels have risen substantially owing to policy support, expansion of domestic distillation capacity, and greater participation of sugar mills and grain- based distilleries. The programme is expected to contribute to multiple national objectives, including lowering greenhouse gas emissions, improving energy security, reducing the country's import bill, and creating additional income opportunities for farmers. Alongside sugarcane-based feedstocks, policymakers have encouraged diversification towards food grains and agricultural residues in order to reduce excessive dependence on a single crop. The initiative forms an important component of India's broader strategy to promote biofuels and a circular economy. Technological developments have also facilitated the introduction of vehicles capable of operating on higher ethanol blends. Nevertheless, experts continue to debate several challenges associated with the programme, including concerns regarding water-intensive cultivation, food security, regional disparities in feedstock availability, and the environmental sustainability of large-scale ethanol production. As India accelerates its clean energy transition, the ethanol blending programme has emerged as an important example of balancing environmental objectives with economic development and rural livelihoods. The success of the initiative will ultimately depend upon technological innovation, sustainable agricultural practices, and the ability to diversify raw materials without compromising food or ecological security.

passages.title: Gaganyaan's Life Support System: Sustaining Human Life in Space
passages.text: Human spaceflight presents engineering challenges that extend far beyond launching a spacecraft into orbit. Once astronauts leave Earth's atmosphere, they enter an environment where breathable air, comfortable temperatures, and safe cabin pressure are unavailable. Unlike satellites, a crewed spacecraft must continuously maintain conditions that allow human beings to survive and perform routine activities throughout the mission. To meet these requirements, India's Gaganyaan programme incorporates an Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS), a complex network of subsystems designed to regulate the spacecraft's internal environment. The system is responsible for maintaining cabin pressure, controlling temperature and humidity, supplying breathable air, and ensuring that contaminants generated during the mission do not accumulate to harmful levels. Continuous monitoring allows onboard conditions to remain within limits suitable for human habitation even as external conditions in space fluctuate dramatically. Given that Gaganyaan is intended as a short-duration mission, its life support architecture has been designed with simplicity, reliability, and safety as guiding principles. Rather than relying extensively on complex regenerative technologies, the system is expected to carry essential consumables for the planned duration of the flight while safely managing waste products until the crew returns to Earth. Such an approach reduces technical complexity and improves mission reliability for India's first human spaceflight programme. The development of the ECLSS represents a significant technological milestone for India's space programme. Beyond supporting the Gaganyaan mission, the experience gained from designing reliable life support technologies is expected to contribute to future long-duration human spaceflight, space stations, and other advanced exploration missions. As India expands its human spaceflight capabilities, mastering environmental control and life support systems will remain fundamental to ensuring crew safety and mission success.

passages.title: India–Nepal Relations: Geography, Security and Contemporary Cooperation
passages.text: India and Nepal share one of South Asia's closest and most distinctive bilateral relationships, shaped by centuries of historical interaction, cultural affinity, and geographical proximity. Their open border facilitates the movement of people, trade, employment, and tourism, making the relationship unique among neighbouring countries. At the same time, certain historical agreements and differing interpretations of territorial boundaries have periodically generated diplomatic discussions, demonstrating the continuing relevance of history in contemporary international relations. Beyond historical ties, Nepal occupies considerable strategic importance in India's security and foreign policy. Situated between two major Asian powers, the country influences the broader geopolitical balance in the Himalayan region. Stability and cooperation between the two neighbours are viewed as essential for regional connectivity, border management, disaster response, and economic development. As a result, both governments maintain regular diplomatic dialogue on issues ranging from infrastructure and energy to security cooperation. Defence collaboration remains an important pillar of bilateral engagement. The armed forces of both countries maintain long-standing institutional ties through regular interactions, professional exchanges, and joint activities aimed at strengthening operational coordination and humanitarian capabilities. Such cooperation reflects the broader objective of enhancing mutual trust while responding effectively to common security and disaster- management challenges. In recent years, India and Nepal have also sought to expand cooperation in sectors such as cross-border connectivity, hydropower, trade, and digital infrastructure. Political developments within Nepal, including changes in government, continue to influence the direction of bilateral engagement, while both countries emphasise dialogue and cooperation as the preferred means of addressing differences. The relationship therefore represents a combination of historical continuity, strategic significance, and evolving regional partnerships.

passages.title: Delimitation and Democratic Representation in India
passages.text: Representative democracy depends not only on periodic elections but also on ensuring that elected representatives speak for populations that are reasonably comparable in size. As demographic patterns change over time because of migration, urbanisation, and population growth, electoral boundaries may require periodic revision so that the principle of equal representation continues to be maintained. Such exercises are intended to strengthen democratic legitimacy while reflecting changes revealed through official population data. In India, the process of revising electoral boundaries is governed by constitutional and statutory provisions designed to ensure impartiality and transparency. An independent authority carries out this exercise after Parliament provides the necessary legal framework. Once the exercise is completed, the revised constituencies become the basis for future elections, contributing to a more balanced system of political representation. The legal framework also seeks to minimise prolonged disputes so that electoral processes are not disrupted by continuous litigation. Recent constitutional developments have renewed public discussion on the relationship between delimitation and political representation. In particular, debates concerning greater inclusiveness in legislatures have highlighted the importance of linking certain constitutional reforms with the completion of future delimitation exercises. These discussions have drawn attention to the broader objective of making representative institutions more inclusive while preserving the constitutional framework governing elections. As India prepares for future demographic changes, delimitation is expected to remain an important constitutional process balancing population shifts, federal considerations, and democratic representation. The subject therefore illustrates how constitutional design, electoral administration, and representative governance work together to sustain a functioning democracy.

passages.title: Critical Minerals and India's Quest for Resource Security
passages.text: The rapid global transition towards cleaner energy systems and advanced technologies has significantly increased demand for a group of minerals that are considered essential for modern industry. These minerals play a crucial role in the manufacture of electric vehicles, renewable energy infrastructure, high-performance electronics, telecommunications equipment, and sophisticated defence technologies. As countries seek to reduce carbon emissions while strengthening technological competitiveness, ensuring reliable access to these resources has become an important strategic objective. Unlike many conventional minerals, the challenge associated with these resources is not limited to their geological availability. Their extraction, processing, refining, and global distribution are often concentrated in a small number of countries, creating vulnerabilities in international supply chains. Recent geopolitical developments have reinforced concerns regarding excessive dependence on limited sources for strategically important raw materials, prompting many nations to diversify imports, encourage domestic exploration, and strengthen international partnerships. India has also intensified efforts to improve long-term resource security by promoting exploration, expanding processing capabilities, encouraging research and recycling, and pursuing cooperation with resource-rich countries abroad. Policymakers increasingly view secure mineral supply chains as essential not only for economic growth but also for energy transition, technological innovation, and national security. As competition for strategic resources grows, countries are adopting comprehensive approaches that combine domestic capability building with international collaboration. These efforts reflect the growing recognition that access to critical minerals will play a decisive role in shaping future industrial development, technological leadership, and global economic resilience.

passages.title: India's Digital Payment Revolution: Building an Inclusive Financial Ecosystem
passages.text: Over the past decade, digital payment systems have transformed the way financial transactions are conducted in India. Advances in digital public infrastructure, increasing smartphone penetration, expanding internet connectivity, and wider access to banking services have enabled millions of individuals and businesses to shift from cash-based transactions to electronic modes of payment. This transformation has contributed to greater financial inclusion while encouraging innovation in the country's rapidly growing financial technology ecosystem. India's digital payments architecture has been designed to promote interoperability, allowing users of different banks and payment applications to transfer funds seamlessly. Such an ecosystem has encouraged competition among service providers while enabling merchants, consumers, and small enterprises to adopt digital payments with minimal infrastructure. The expansion of digital transactions has also supported formalisation of the economy by creating reliable digital records that can facilitate access to financial services, including credit for small businesses. As digital payment systems continue to expand, policymakers are increasingly focusing on strengthening cybersecurity, consumer protection, and the resilience of payment infrastructure. At the same time, efforts are being made to improve cross-border payment connectivity and extend the benefits of digital finance to international travellers and other eligible users. These developments reflect India's broader objective of building secure, efficient, and globally interoperable digital public infrastructure. Despite remarkable progress, challenges remain. Uneven digital literacy, disparities in internet access, and the dominance of a limited number of service providers continue to generate important policy debates. Addressing these issues is considered essential for ensuring that future growth in digital payments remains competitive, inclusive, and secure.

passages.title: Supreme Court of India — Judges, Jurisdiction and Constitutional Framework
passages.text: The constitutional design of India seeks to maintain an institutional balance among different organs of the State. The judiciary occupies a distinctive position within this framework because courts are entrusted not only with resolving disputes but also with interpreting constitutional provisions and protecting legally guaranteed rights. The higher judiciary therefore operates within a structure that combines judicial authority with safeguards intended to protect institutional independence. The Constitution establishes the Supreme Court as the highest judicial forum in the country and provides a framework concerning its composition, appointment of judges, conditions of service and jurisdiction. At the same time, several aspects of the Court's institutional functioning are capable of being regulated by Parliament through legislation. This arrangement allows the constitutional framework to remain relatively stable while permitting adjustments to respond to changing institutional requirements. Judicial independence does not imply that judges are beyond constitutional accountability. The Constitution establishes specific procedures concerning appointment, tenure and removal. These procedures are designed to prevent arbitrary interference while ensuring that constitutional office-holders remain subject to institutional checks. The process of appointment has also acquired a significant judicial dimension through constitutional interpretation over several decades. The jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is similarly diverse. It can adjudicate certain disputes involving constitutional entities, hear appeals from lower judicial and quasi-judicial bodies, and exercise powers intended to ensure substantial justice in appropriate cases. It may also perform an advisory function when constitutional conditions for seeking its opinion are fulfilled. The constitutional position of the judiciary must therefore be understood as a combination of authority and restraint. Courts exercise considerable powers, but these powers operate within procedures and institutional relationships established by the Constitution.

passages.title: G7 Summit 2026 and India
passages.text: The 2026 G7 Summit brought together leaders of the major industrialised democracies to discuss contemporary global challenges. The summit included an Outreach Session, through which countries beyond the core grouping were invited to participate in discussions concerning international cooperation and global priorities. India used the platform to highlight concerns of the Global South, including the need for greater participation of developing and middle-income countries in global decision-making. It also emphasised the importance of strengthening international trust and developing partnerships based on mutual respect and shared responsibility. Alongside its participation in the summit discussions, India held bilateral meetings with several partner countries. These engagements covered areas such as trade, investment, security, energy and strategic cooperation. India and one of its major North American partners discussed strengthening their economic relationship and advancing negotiations for a comprehensive trade arrangement. The G7 has evolved considerably since its creation in the 1970s. It functions differently from treaty-based international organisations and operates through an annual presidency system. The country holding the presidency plays a significant role in determining priorities and organising meetings. The grouping also maintains engagement with countries outside its core membership through outreach mechanisms. The European Union participates in G7 proceedings through its institutional leadership, although its status differs from that of the individual countries constituting the grouping.

passages.title: Uttarakhand Becomes India’s Sixth Fully Literate State
passages.text: Uttarakhand has achieved an important milestone in adult education by becoming the sixth state in India to be declared fully literate under the country’s national adult literacy initiative. The achievement reflects the state’s efforts to provide learning opportunities to adults who were unable to acquire adequate education through the formal schooling system. The initiative adopts a broader understanding of literacy. Rather than limiting literacy to the ability to read and write, it seeks to develop foundational learning, numeracy and practical skills that enable adults to participate more effectively in everyday social and economic activities. Digital and financial awareness are also important components of this broader approach. The programme relies on the participation of volunteers, educators, local institutions and communities to identify learners and support their learning. Technology is used to facilitate registration, provide learning resources and monitor progress. The declaration of a state as fully literate is based on measurable learning outcomes, rather than simply counting the number of people enrolled in literacy programmes. This makes the achievement an indicator of actual progress in foundational learning. Uttarakhand’s achievement is significant in the wider context of India’s efforts to reduce adult illiteracy and expand opportunities for lifelong learning. It demonstrates how community participation, institutional support and technology-enabled education can contribute to improving literacy outcomes among adults who were previously excluded from formal education.

passages.title: The Commonwealth Games
passages.text: The Commonwealth Games traces its roots to 1930. Originally styled as the British Empire Games, it was later renamed the Commonwealth Games and is today governed by the Commonwealth Games Federation. The closest edition, staged in a major Scottish city in 2026, was deliberately scaled down to a compact format of ten sports, dropping several disciplines that had appeared in earlier editions. A unicorn served as the official mascot, chosen in honour of the host nation's national animal. Competing against a much reduced roster that left out several of its strongest disciplines, the Indian contingent still delivered an efficient campaign, finishing in the middle of the leading pack with thirty-nine medals-thirteen gold, seventeen silver and nine bronze. A long-distance runner made history by becoming the first Indian to claim two medals in a single edition, and a weightlifter sealed three consecutive golds across as many Games. Looking ahead, the next edition, scheduled for 2030, is expected to celebrate the centenary of the event's founding and is set to be held in a country that hosted it once before, in its capital city.

passages.title: Komagata Maru Incident
passages.text: The incident involving a chartered steamship in the early twentieth century was a pivotal event in the global history of the Indian freedom struggle, highlighting the racial exclusion faced by Indian immigrants in British dominions and the subsequent radicalisation of transnational revolutionary movements. The vessel was chartered by a prominent activist to deliberately challenge exclusionary immigration laws. These regulations mandated that incoming immigrants arrive directly from their country of birth or nationality via a continuous journey on through-tickets. Because non-stop naval routes from India to North America were virtually non-existent, the law served as a hidden mechanism to restrict South Asian entry. Upon reaching its destination port in North America, the ship was denied permission to dock, and only a tiny fraction of passengers who could demonstrate previous legal residency were permitted to disembark. Local expatriate communities mobilized to form a dedicated body to offer relief and launch a legal battle, though local courts ultimately upheld the exclusionary mandates. The vessel was eventually forced to depart under armed naval escort. The crisis reached a tragic climax upon the vessel's return to India. When local colonial authorities attempted to restrict the passengers' movement, tensions escalated into open violence, resulting in multiple casualties and mass detentions. This confrontation acted as a major catalyst for overseas Indian revolutionaries, convincing many that constitutional agitation was ineffective and driving increased support for armed resistance against colonial rule.

passages.title: India–Nepal Border Dispute: Lipulekh Pass & The Kailash Mansarovar Yatra
passages.text: In 2026, an annual event of deep religious significance once again placed one of South Asia's oldest and most sensitive boundary disputes in the spotlight. When India announced the resumption of the famous Himalayan pilgrimage to two sacred sites, using a high-altitude mountain pass in the Kumaon region of Uttarakhand as one of its principal gateways, the government of Nepal formally objected — to New Delhi and, notably, to the third country that controls the far side of the pass, which lies at the junction of the borders of three nations. The dispute traces back more than two centuries, to a treaty signed in the aftermath of an Anglo-Nepalese war. That treaty fixed Nepal's boundary along the course of a river, but the two neighbours have never agreed on precisely where that river begins. India maintains that the river rises near a particular valley, placing the contested settlements — including the strategically important pass itself within Indian territory; Nepal contends that its source lies further west, which would place all of the disputed places within Nepal. Because both countries read the same treaty differently, the boundary has never been definitively settled. The disagreement was sharply aggravated in 2020, when India inaugurated a road through the disputed area and Nepal, in response, formally incorporated the territories into its official map. The latest friction over the pilgrimage route reflects a recurring tension: New Delhi insists it has used the pass for the pilgrimage for decades, while Kathmandu argues that no bilateral arrangement with the third country can legitimise the use of territory it claims as its own.

passages.title: India's 100th Ramsar Site & The Ramsar Convention
passages.text: In 2026, India crossed a symbolic conservation milestone when the Prime Minister announced, that a bird sanctuary in a north-Indian state had been designated as the country's hundredth Ramsar site. The wetland, named after a local lake and home to rich avifaunal diversity attracting numerous migratory and resident birds, became the entry that took India's tally into three figures. Shortly afterwards, the count rose again when a lake in a hill state in the far north-east — the first wetland of that state to earn the designation — was added, taking the national total past one hundred. The Ramsar Convention, under which such sites are designated, is an international treaty for the conservation and sustainable use of wetlands, signed in a city of the same name in the early 1970s. India became a party to the treaty in 1982, and its network of designated wetlands has since grown from a handful of sites to become the largest such network in Asia and the third-largest in the world. The sites span everything from high-altitude Himalayan lakes and coastal mangroves to human-made reservoirs and bird sanctuaries. India's largest designated wetland is a vast mangrove ecosystem on the eastern coast, home to a famous tiger population. Several of the sites lie along a major migratory-bird flyway, and a few are listed on a special register of wetlands facing significant ecological stress.

passages.title: El Niño and The Economic Threat to India
passages.text: A strengthening El Niño has emerged as an important economic concern for India in 2026. The World Meteorological Organization expects the event to influence global temperature and rainfall patterns during the latter half of the year. The India Meteorological Department has also projected below-normal rainfall during the second half of the southwest monsoon season, although the eventual impact will depend on when and where the rain falls. A national rainfall figure can hide substantial regional differences. Rain received after the principal sowing period may not compensate farmers for an earlier dry spell, while excessive rain in one region cannot remove water stress elsewhere. Weak or irregular rainfall can delay planting, reduce yields, increase irrigation expenses and affect reservoir and groundwater levels. The consequences can spread beyond agriculture. Lower farm incomes may weaken rural purchases of consumer goods, vehicles and construction materials. Reduced crop supplies can increase food-processing and retail costs, while greater agricultural imports may put pressure on the trade balance. Higher food expenditure also leaves households with less income for other goods and services. For policymakers, a climate-related supply shock creates a difficult balance. Measures that suppress demand cannot produce additional crops, while excessive stimulus may strengthen price pressures. The government may therefore combine monetary caution with crop-contingency plans, trade measures, public food-stock management and targeted income support. Irrigation coverage, crop diversification, storage facilities and accurate seasonal forecasts determine whether the climatic disturbance remains manageable. El Niño should consequently be treated as a risk multiplier rather than a guaranteed economic crisis. Its final effect depends not only on oceanic conditions but also on domestic preparedness, regional rainfall distribution, global commodity prices and the speed of policy intervention. Prepared with reference to reports from the WMO, IMD and RBI.

passages.title: Third India–Nordic Summit, 2026
passages.text: The Third India–Nordic Summit, held on 19 May 2026, marked a significant expansion of India’s engagement with northern Europe. The participating leaders elevated the relationship to Strategic Partnership, seeking to combine India’s market, manufacturing capacity and skilled workforce with Nordic expertise in sustainability and advanced technology. The discussions covered renewable energy, green hydrogen, low-emission industries, water management and the circular economy. Maritime cooperation included green shipping, shipbuilding, sustainable ship recycling and ocean-based industries. The leaders also supported deeper collaboration between universities, laboratories, start- ups and business incubators, including research in emerging communication technologies. Trade and investment formed another important component. The leaders proposed using India’s recent trade arrangements with European partners to improve market access, encourage investment and create resilient supply chains. Nordic firms were invited to explore opportunities in India’s green transition, defence manufacturing and financial-services ecosystem. Greater movement of students, researchers and skilled professionals was also encouraged. The partnership has a wider strategic dimension. Changes in the polar region affect climate systems, shipping routes and access to natural resources, making scientific cooperation increasingly important. India and the Nordic countries consequently supported joint polar research and continued engagement through established multilateral institutions. They also discussed the conflicts in Europe and West Asia, terrorism and the need to reform global governance institutions. The summit reflects a broader diplomatic strategy in which India works with small but technologically advanced economies on issue-specific cooperation. Nordic countries possess substantial expertise and investment capital but comparatively limited domestic markets. India offers scale and talent but requires technology and long-term financing for its development transition. Converting summit declarations into projects will depend on regulatory certainty, protection of intellectual property, commercial viability and the ability to manage geopolitical differences.

passages.title: A Guarantee Reforged
passages.text: Replacing the old statute has meant rewriting the financial compact between Delhi and the states. Under the earlier law, the Centre alone paid the unskilled wage bill, and entitlements generated expenditure without limit. The new one makes the states partners in cost: for most states the wage bill is split three parts to two — the larger share borne by the Centre; for the hill states of the north-east and the Himalayas the split is nine parts to one; and for union territories without legislatures of their own, the Centre still pays the whole. The scheme thereby changes character — from a purely central scheme to a shared one, in which the Centre sets the standards and the states execute, within a predictable ceiling of central funds beyond which the state itself must pay. The works themselves have been pulled out of their old scattering into four named priority verticals: securing water — harvesting rain, recharging the ground; building the core of rural infrastructure, the roads and connectivity that open markets; raising livelihood assets — storage, markets, units of production; and, in the fourth, hardening the countryside against extreme weather, with flood drainage and soil conservation. Planning runs from the bottom up but is wired into national systems: every village panchayat prepares its own development plan, and every asset created is pooled into a single national register of rural infrastructure, connected with the country's grand spatial masterplan for connectivity. Oversight is being digitised — artificial intelligence and biometric checks to catch irregularities early, satellite tracking of works, live dashboards, weekly public disclosures, and social audits twice a year — while the worker's old protections survive: if work is not provided in time, an allowance must be paid.

passages.title: Scoring The Global GoalS
passages.text: In 2015 the world's governments adopted a blueprint for the following fifteen years: an agenda of seventeen sustainable development goals, from ending poverty and hunger to protecting the planet and strengthening global partnership. Performance against that agenda is measured each year by an international index, which scores and ranks the participating countries. The annual verdicts have been sobering. Even the countries that habitually lead the table remain far from their own targets, and at the present pace the majority of the goals will be missed across the world by the agreed deadline. India is a participant in every edition of that assessment, and its results are followed closely at home, where each release renews a familiar debate about how far the country has travelled and how far it still has to go. Commentary tends to turn on the same few points: the distance between India's score and the leading countries, the comparison with its regional neighbours, and the unevenness of progress across the goals themselves — with those tied to everyday well-being, such as poverty, hunger and nutrition, health, and water and sanitation, receiving the closest attention. The honest summary is one of persistence rather than completion; the targets of 2030 remain ahead. Measurement, however, is a machinery of its own. Alongside the global index, each country maintains a national framework of indicators, and the periodic progress reports that track them are compiled at home, institution by institution. The arrangement echoes an older architecture: the framework that preceded the present agenda carried a far smaller set of goals and targets, and the successor agenda deliberately enlarged both. As the ambition has grown, so has the business of counting it.

passages.title: 60th Jnanpith Award
passages.text: India has many prizes for literature, but one sits clearly above the rest. The country's highest literary honour is conferred each year upon a living writer, in recognition of a distinguished body of work rather than a single book. It is administered by a cultural trust with roots in the world of newspapers and publishing, and it is decided not by any ministry but by a jury of writers, critics and scholars, drawing on nominations gathered through literary bodies across the land as well as from individual men and women of letters. The list of recipients reads like a gallery of modern Indian writing: poets, novelists, short-story writers and essayists, and even authors whose words have reached the public through theatre, film and song. Laureates come from every region of the country and write in many of its languages, so that each conferment honours not only an individual but also the literary tradition that formed them. On occasion the prize has gone to women writers — a fact recalled with pride whenever the honour's history is recounted. Every announcement revives familiar debates: whether the jury has chosen wisely, whether some languages are represented more generously than others, and which great name has been made to wait the longest. Yet the award's standing is never really in question. The news of the selection is awaited across the country, the laureate is celebrated at gatherings and in the press, and the prize is presented at a formal ceremony often witnessed by the nation's highest dignitaries. For a new generation of writers, the honour remains what it has always been: the distant, shining summit of a literary life.

passages.title: A Question Of Representation
passages.text:
India's constitutional map is far from uniform. Alongside the states stand the union territories, run by the Union through appointed officials. Most have no elected legislature; only a small number do, and the national capital enjoys a distinctive arrangement — a directly elected assembly and a council of ministers over a defined list of subjects, while the Union keeps public order, police and land. That arrangement was added by amendment decades after independence.

The same asymmetry lies at the heart of a grievance in the country's far north. In 2019 the former state there was split into two union territories: one kept an elected government, while the other — a high, cold Himalayan region — was placed directly under the Centre, with no assembly of its own. Residents who had once sent members to the state legislature now found decisions in appointed hands; local councils existed, but their powers fell far short of a legislature's. Campaigners call the result a representation deficit, and their demands — full statehood, seats in Parliament, a recruitment commission, safeguards for tribal identity and a fragile ecology — keep the region in the news. The Constitution, however, offers models of self-rule for tribal communities. In the north-east a special constitutional schedule created autonomous district councils for tribal areas of four states, empowered to legislate on land, forests, water, trade, marriage and customs, and to run village courts and schools. A parallel framework elsewhere gives village assemblies a decisive say over local resources. Advocates for the Himalayan territory argue that a comparable arrangement could secure local identity and national frontiers; the government, wary of constitutional complexity, prefers to strengthen the councils that exist and to protect local residents by regulation. The disagreement is over how much self-rule a strategically vital region can safely be given.

passages.title: Remembering A Constitutional Crisis
passages.text: Constitutions are written against the memory of failure, and the Indian Constitution is no exception. It arms the Union with special powers intended for times of grave peril, yet it also assumes that such powers will be used sparingly and ended promptly. For about two years in the middle of the 1970s that assumption failed. The freedoms guaranteed by the Constitution were suspended on a vast scale: thousands of citizens — parliamentarians, journalists, students and workers — were detained without trial; the press was censored; the courts were pressed into acquiescence; Parliament was reduced to silence. What the framers had conceived as a last-resort fortress became the instrument of one party's rule. The memory of those years has been institutionalised. In the mid-2020s the government began observing a designated day each year, falling in the same season as the original events, to honour those who resisted and suffered and to pledge that such abuse never recur. Official programmes, exhibitions, publications and films mark the day, addressed by the country's most senior leaders. Opposition parties mark the same date in their own way, so the period has become a recurring touchstone of the country's political memory. The constitutional legacy is double-edged. One amendment, unmatched in sweep, recast the document's basic features; a corrective amendment under a successor government later restored much of what had been changed, narrowed the ground on which national power could be suspended, and returned legislatures to their ordinary terms. The detentions had rested on a preventive-detention statute long since repealed. Scholars debate whether the episode was an aberration of individuals or a warning about the fragility of legal safeguards. What is certain is that it remains the reference point for arguments about the limits of constitutional power.

passages.title: A Region Arranges Its Own Security
passages.text: West Asia is rearranging its own security. For decades the region's order rested on the promise of protection from a distant superpower, and much of it still does; but repeated rounds of escalation have made that promise look less dependable and have pushed several of its powers to hedge. The clearest expression of the mood came in 2026, when three regional states signed a joint defence agreement in the holy city of Makkah. The compact commits their armed forces to regular joint training and a structured exchange of intelligence and threat assessments — the machinery of closer military cooperation, not a declaration of war. The motives of the signatories are not identical, but they overlap. Attacks on shipping in the Red Sea, drone and missile fire that has exposed the limits of existing defences, and the fragility of the narrow sea passages through which the world's energy moves have fed a sense of exposure. One member, whose revenues rest heavily on energy exports, inward investment, tourism and an ambitious domestic transformation programme, has concluded that reliance on an outside patron is no longer enough and that independent defensive capability must be built. Analysts are careful, however, not to overstate the pact. Its operational provisions remain thin, its enforcement mechanisms unclear, and the alignments it creates cut across older rivalries in the region; it should therefore be read as a statement of intent rather than a formal treaty of the Western kind. Scepticism does not lessen its significance. The emergence of a self-arranged security compact among regional powers signals a slow shift in the balance of West Asia, and its consequences reach beyond the region — to India, whose energy security, defence exports, connectivity projects and standing in the Indian Ocean are all bound up in what happens there.

passages.title: Nepal Floods and Himalayan Disaster Vulnerability
passages.text: In August 2026, Nepal experienced one of its most devastating recent flood disasters, highlighting the vulnerability of Himalayan communities to sudden and extreme natural hazards. The disaster affected settlements, transport networks, border infrastructure and economic activities, while rescue operations were complicated by difficult terrain, damaged roads and continuing geological instability. The event drew attention to the complex interaction between high-altitude geological processes, ice and water systems in the Himalayas. Experts linked the disaster to a sudden mountain event that generated a powerful flood wave carrying large quantities of water, mud and debris downstream. The rapid movement of the flood left limited time for communities and authorities to respond, highlighting the limitations of existing early-warning mechanisms in remote mountain environments. The consequences extended well beyond loss of life and displacement. Roads, bridges, markets, communication facilities and energy infrastructure were damaged. Nepal's heavy dependence on hydropower made the impact particularly significant, with numerous energy facilities affected and many workers requiring rescue. The disaster demonstrated how damage to infrastructure in mountainous terrain can produce cascading effects on electricity supply, transportation and emergency access. Rescue operations were especially challenging because many people were stranded in difficult-to-access locations, including underground infrastructure. Specialized tunnel-rescue capabilities, engineering equipment, aerial surveys and coordinated search operations consequently became important elements of the response. International assistance also played a significant role in supporting Nepal's rescue efforts. The disaster also underscored the importance of regional cooperation in Himalayan disaster management. Nepal's geographical position and close links with neighbouring countries make cross-border coordination, information sharing and early-warning systems particularly important. The 2026 floods therefore highlighted the need to move beyond post-disaster relief towards hazard mapping, resilient infrastructure, improved early-warning systems and stronger regional disaster-response mechanisms.

passages.title: Regulation of Mineral Rights and Mineral-Bearing Lands
passages.text: India's mineral sector is governed principally by the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, a statute that sits at the intersection of the Union and the States in India's fiscal federal structure. Mining- related subjects are distributed between the Union and State Lists of the Seventh Schedule, and questions repeatedly arise over which level of government may regulate which activity, and over which level may tax what. These questions have acquired sharpness in recent years because several States revised and multiplied the charges they assessed on the sector, and because a nine-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court in 2024 examined the boundary between a tax and the other payments collected from the sector, and also addressed the recovery of outstanding dues. The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 was passed by both Houses on 13 August 2026. It amends the 1957 Act on three related fronts: the reach of the Central regulatory framework, the power of State Governments to impose charges connected with mineral rights, and the legal position of claims that existed before the amendment came into force. On the first front, the amendment extends the range of subjects that fall within the framework laid down by the principal Act by adding a new category of land to the matters already regulated under it. The statute supplies a definition for this category, and the parameters used to identify it are to be settled through the framework that the Act itself provides. Supporters of the change argue that mineral resources are finite, that their exploitation carries national and strategic consequences, and that a single regulatory architecture produces better outcomes for exploration than a patchwork of arrangements. On the second front, the amendment introduces a fresh provision into the principal Act governing charges that State Governments may impose in connection with mineral rights or with the category of land brought within the Act's scope. The provision is drafted broadly as to the names such charges may be given, and it subjects them to a framework whose operation is governed elsewhere in the statutory scheme. The provision also engages with demands raised by States for periods before the amendment took effect. On the third front, the amendment prescribes transitional treatment for the claims that existed when it came into force. It separates such claims into categories and attaches a distinct legal consequence to each category, so that the status of past and outstanding demands is settled rather than left to litigation. Rule-making authority under the Act is correspondingly adjusted, so that the framework applicable to permissible State-level charges is furnished through a single mechanism rather than through separately drafted instruments in different States. Taken together, the amendment is presented as a measure intended to secure uniformity, predictability and stability in the fiscal and regulatory treatment of mineral resources, and thereby to support exploration and investment in the sector.

passages.title: Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit 2026
passages.text: The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) remains an important multilateral platform bringing together countries across Eurasia. Its cooperation extends across areas such as regional security, counter-terrorism, connectivity, economic cooperation, technology, culture and people-to-people exchanges. The organisation has also developed various mechanisms involving ministers, experts, youth and other stakeholders. The 26th meeting of the Council of Heads of State was held in 2026 as the culmination of the organisation's annual chairmanship cycle. The summit adopted a declaration covering a range of regional and international issues, including terrorism, connectivity, scientific cooperation, climate-related concerns and economic development. Member states also reaffirmed their commitment to cooperation based on sovereignty, equality and mutual respect. India used the summit to emphasise its priorities within the organisation. Prime Minister Narendra Modi highlighted the importance of strengthening cooperation in security, connectivity and opportunities for development. He also stressed the role of technology, entrepreneurship, innovation, start-ups and youth engagement in expanding cooperation among SCO countries. India further placed emphasis on civilisational and people-to-people exchanges. Several India-led initiatives relating to youth, science, literature and cultural dialogue received attention during the summit. The proposed Civilisation Dialogue mechanism was presented as a platform for encouraging greater interaction among the diverse societies represented within the organisation. The summit also reaffirmed the SCO's institutional character. While security remains a major area of cooperation, the organisation does not function as a conventional collective-defence arrangement. Its agenda combines security concerns with economic, technological, cultural and developmental priorities. The meeting also marked the transition to the next annual chairmanship cycle, demonstrating the SCO's rotating institutional structure and its continuing emphasis on multilateral cooperation across Eurasia.

passages.title: Cauvery Water Dispute and Its Institutional Framework
passages.text: The Cauvery river water dispute is a major inter-State water-sharing issue involving Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry. Its constitutional foundation lies in the provisions concerning disputes over waters of inter-State rivers, while Parliament has enacted legislation to provide mechanisms for adjudication and implementation. Following the Supreme Court's 2018 judgment, the Union Government framed the Cauvery Water Management Scheme, 2018 under the existing statutory framework. The scheme established institutional arrangements for implementing the Tribunal's award as modified by the Court and for regulating water releases among the concerned parties. The Authority established under the scheme has a multi-member composition, with specified qualifications and tenure provisions for its leadership and members. It is intended to facilitate coordinated implementation and monitoring of water-sharing arrangements among the concerned States. The Supreme Court's 2018 decision also modified the earlier allocation of Cauvery waters, taking into account factors including drinking-water requirements and groundwater availability. The revised arrangement subsequently formed the basis for implementation and monitoring. The dispute continues to influence irrigation, drinking water, hydropower and infrastructure development in the basin. Proposals involving additional storage and water-supply infrastructure have therefore remained subject to scrutiny by relevant authorities. One such proposal has involved a proposed balancing reservoir and drinking- water project, for which the Central Water Commission sought inputs from the institutional mechanism established under the 2018 arrangement.

passages.title: Vikram-1 and India’s Private Space Launch Capability
passages.text: India’s space sector has witnessed rapid growth in private participation following reforms that opened several activities to non-governmental entities. This transformation has encouraged Indian start-ups to develop launch vehicles, satellites, propulsion systems and other space technologies, complementing the capabilities of the national space programme. A major milestone in this process came in July 2026, when a privately developed launch vehicle undertook its maiden orbital mission from an Indian launch facility. The mission successfully demonstrated the ability of an Indian private company to place payloads into Low Earth Orbit (LEO), marking an important step in the development of a commercially oriented launch ecosystem. The launch vehicle incorporates several advanced technologies aimed at reducing structural mass and improving manufacturing efficiency. Its design combines composite structures, solid propulsion and an additively manufactured liquid engine, reflecting the increasing use of innovative manufacturing techniques in India's private space industry. The maiden mission carried a range of payloads, including satellites and technology-demonstration experiments from different private-sector entities. These payloads illustrated the growing diversity of applications supported by small launch vehicles, including satellite deployment, technological experimentation and emerging orbital services. Beyond its technical objectives, the mission also carried symbolic elements intended to connect India's contemporary space ambitions with the country's scientific heritage. Such initiatives highlight the role of private space companies not merely in commercial launch services but also in promoting public engagement with science and India's broader space journey.
