passages.title: Indonesia's Volcanic Eruption & the Ring of Fire
passages.text:
On September 2026, a small volcanic island rising out of the narrow waterway that separates Java from Sumatra began hurling lava fountains and booming across the region. By Sunday, a second ash cloud had punched fifty thousand feet into the sky, drifting over Banten, Lampung and Bengkulu provinces and out across the Indian Ocean. Ash was detected in the airspace over the capital, forcing authorities to shut Jakarta's main international gateway along with several other airports; over 1,500 flights were grounded, schools in the capital moved their classes online, and services as far away as Bali and Medan were disrupted. The Transport Minister, Dudy Purwagandhi, conceded that no one could say when the disruption would end "due to the dynamic weather." Mercifully, no casualties were reported, no evacuation was ordered the nearest settlement lies over sixteen kilometres away — and, unlike the December 2018 episode when this very volcano demonstrated that it could kill hundreds without the warning of an earthquake, no tsunami alert was issued this time.

The volcano itself is a child in geological terms, having emerged from the sea less than a century ago, growing out of the submerged caldera left behind by its parent, whose late-nineteenth-century explosion remains among the loudest sounds in recorded history and altered global climate for years. Its alert status had already been raised to Level III in July 2026 after a surge in activity, even as Java's highest peak continued its own months-long eruption further east. None of this is unusual for Indonesia, the country with more active volcanoes than any other, sitting on the world's most violent tectonic arc — a horseshoe of subduction zones that hosts the overwhelming majority of the planet's earthquakes and eruptions.

passages.title: The Indus Waters Treaty & The Hague Ruling
passages.text:
Few treaties have survived what this one has — three full-scale wars, decades of frozen diplomacy, and repeated military crises — which is precisely why its present limbo is so consequential. Signed in Karachi more than six decades ago after nearly a decade of negotiations brokered by an international financial institution, the agreement performed a surgical division of a river system: the three eastern rivers for unrestricted use by India, the three western rivers largely for the lower riparian, leaving India roughly one-fifth of the system's waters along with narrowly defined rights to run-of-the-river hydroelectricity upstream.

That architecture cracked in the spring of 2025, when gunmen massacred twenty-six tourists in a Kashmir meadow. Within a day, New Delhi announced that the treaty would be held "in abeyance" until its neighbour "credibly and irrevocably" abjured support for cross-border terrorism a word, critics noted, that appears nowhere in the treaty or in the law of treaties. Islamabad moved the arbitral tribunal, which conducted hearings at the Peace Palace in April 2026 without India, which has consistently branded the forum "illegally constituted" and boycotted its proceedings since 2016-era objections hardened.

On 31 August 2026, the five-member court ruled unanimously that the treaty contains no exit hatch for one party alone: it can be modified or terminated only by another duly ratified treaty between the two states. Testing India's justifications against international law material breach, fundamental change of circumstances, armed conflict, countermeasures it found none sufficient. The treaty, it declared, "remains fully in force." Alongside the award came interim measures concerning a contested hydroelectric plant, crafted to prevent construction from creating irreversible facts on the ground before a parallel technical process, expected to conclude in mid-2027, delivers its verdict. New Delhi rejected the award within hours; the abeyance, it said, stands. (Extracted, with edits and revision, from reports of Reuters and legal commentaries, September 2026)

passages.title: India–UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA)
passages.text:
When the agreement finally entered into force on 15 July 2026, it ended a wait that had stretched across three British Prime Ministers and fourteen rounds of negotiations begun in January 2022. The pact itself had been signed almost a year earlier, during the Indian Prime Minister's visit to Britain, at the countryside retreat of his host — the two commerce ministers putting pen to paper as both leaders looked on, and a ten-year roadmap for the wider relationship was unveiled alongside.

India's Commerce Minister has called it the country's "most comprehensive" trade pact ever, and a "template" for those to come. The architecture explains the enthusiasm: nearly all of India's export lines enter Britain duty- free from day one, sweeping away the four-to-sixteen per cent handicap that Indian garments, footwear, carpets, marine and processed food products suffered against zero-duty competitors from Bangladesh, Pakistan and Cambodia an opening into a market worth over five hundred billion dollars, with bilateral trade, currently around fifty-six billion dollars, projected to double by the end of the decade.

Britain's prize lies in what India has historically defended hardest. Tariffs on its most celebrated spirit the bulk of which, ironically, is imported by Indian blenders themselves are halved at once, gliding down further over a decade above a minimum import price. For the first time in any Indian trade agreement, steep duty cuts were conceded on fully built foreign cars, though within calibrated quotas, and with electric vehicles shielded for the first five years. India also opened, for the first time, tens of thousands of high-value central government contracts to British bidders. Yet each side kept a jealously guarded exclusion list, and a companion convention on an entirely different subject travelled with the treaty into force the same day proof that modern trade deals are about far more than tariffs. (Extracted, with edits and revision, from reports of The Times of India, The New Indian Express and PIB, July 2026)

passages.title: India's First Hydrogen Train & Green Hydrogen Push
passages.text:
When the Prime Minister flagged off the gleaming ten-coach rake from a junction station in Haryana's hinterland in July 2026, Indian Railways crossed a threshold it had been approaching for years: its first train to run on a fuel whose only exhaust is water vapour. The train now shuttles along an 89-kilometre section, calling at about a dozen stations on a route that passes through Gohana,  a capacity that has allowed the national transporter to claim a world record for such a train on the broad gauge, since most hydrogen trains elsewhere are two- or three- car units on narrower networks.

The engineering is entirely home-grown. Designed and built at a coach factory in southern India that has been the cradle of the country's train-set revolution, the rake carries a driving power car at each end, each generating 1,200 kilowatts of traction through fuel cells paired with lithium iron phosphate batteries. It is fed from the

Railways' largest hydrogen refuelling facility, built at the originating station itself, where water is split by electrolysis, compressed to 500 bar, and dispensed at 350 bar through two independent dispensers so that both power cars can be fuelled simultaneously.

The pilot is the vanguard of a larger scheme under which the Railways intends to run dozens of such trains on hill and heritage routes where stringing electric wires would deface landscapes that in several cases carry global recognition at a sanctioned cost of about eighty crore rupees per train. The experiment also plugs into a national mission, approved in 2023 with an outlay short of twenty thousand crore rupees, that aims to make the country a global hub for producing a fuel the world has begun to treat as the currency of deep decarbonisation.

passages.title: The Anti-Paper Leak Law & Its 2026 Strengthening
passages.text:
Few pieces of legislation have travelled from cabinet table to both Houses of Parliament as quickly. Approved by the Union Cabinet on a Friday in late July 2026, circulated among Members the following day, introduced in the Lok Sabha on Monday by the Minister of State for Personnel, and passed by both Houses within the same week the amendment Bill was born of a crisis. Weeks of nationwide student protests over the alleged leak of a national medical entrance paper had already claimed a political casualty: the Education Minister had resigned, and his successor found himself defending the Bill through nearly eight hours of stormy debate, walkouts, and repeated adjournments in the Upper House.

The parent statute it amends is itself young enacted only in 2024, as India's first central law criminalising unfair means in public examinations, covering tests conducted by the major central recruitment and entrance bodies. But the events of 2026 convinced the government that its deterrents were too gentle. The amendment therefore raises the floor and the ceiling: for individuals, both the minimum and maximum terms of imprisonment go up, alongside a five-fold increase in fine; for organised examination crime, the minimum term is lengthened and the minimum fine multiplied ten-fold; for service providers — the companies that run centres, supply technology and manage logistics the maximum fine rises five-fold and the period of debarment from public examinations doubles.

Equally significant is the procedural machinery: investigations must now conclude within a fixed two-month timeline, Special Fast Track Courts are to be created for time-bound trials, and Special Task Forces will target organised syndicates. Critics in Parliament asked a harder question whether severity of punishment alone can secure what administration has failed to: the sanctity of the examination hall. After being passed by both Houses, the Bill received presidential assent in August 2026, bringing the strengthened framework into force.

passages.title: The Aravalli Ruling Defining a Mountain to Save It
passages.text:
How high must a hill be before the law will protect it? That deceptively simple question reached the Supreme Court because India's oldest mountain chain — a weathered spine of rock older than the Himalayas by well over a billion years — had for decades been governed by a patchwork of definitions across the states it traverses. In November 2025, a Bench headed by the then Chief Justice of India accepted a uniform, elevation-based formula proposed by a committee led by the Union Environment Ministry: a landform would qualify as a hill of the range if it rose at least one hundred metres above the surrounding local terrain, and two or more such hills within five hundred metres of each other would together constitute the range. One state, interestingly, had been following a similar height criterion since 2006.

The Court refused to impose a blanket ban on mining, reasoning as it had in an earlier judgment of 2021 that outright prohibition breeds illegality rather than protection. Instead, it froze all new mining leases until a comprehensive Management Plan for Sustainable Mining is prepared by a designated forestry research body, modelled on the plan earlier created for a forest in Jharkhand. Exceptions were carved for minerals bearing on strategic and national interests. The Court underscored what was at stake: the range is a green barrier holding back the eastward creep of a great desert, and a lung for the national capital region.

Then came the storm. Critics alleged the height threshold would strip protection from the vast majority of the range's lower hillocks, dismantling safeguards traceable to a 1992 notification. Within weeks, the Court took suo motu cognisance of the row, constituted a fresh expert body, and the Union ministry directed states to ban new leases across the entire landscape. In September 2026, the Court refused that body more time, demanding its report by the end of November.

passages.title: Ramon Magsaysay Awards 2026
passages.text:
Coinciding with the 119th birth anniversary of the seventh President of the Philippines, the Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation formally announced its 2026 laureates last August 31. Since its inception in 1958, the Ramon Magsaysay Award has grown into what is widely regarded as Asia’s premier prize and highest honour. The foundation seeks to recognise individuals and organisations whose integrity, courage and selfless service have directly improved lives.

During a global livestream broadcast from Manila, the foundation confirmed the selection of three individuals for the 2026 roster. While the winners operate in drastically different fields, the Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation selected them based on a shared ethos. Edgar O Chua, chairperson of the foundation, noted this connection during the announcement.

“For sixty-eight years, the Ramon Magsaysay Award has celebrated transformative leaders who have become enduring builders of a better future for Asia and the world,” Chua stated. “Each generation of Ramon Magsaysay Awardees has shown us that integrity, courage, and compassion can shape societies for the better. This year’s recipients stand firmly by that proud tradition.”

passages.title: 18th BRICS Summit 2026
passages.text:
The 18th BRICS Summit, under the presidency of India, began in New Delhi. Prime Minister Modi welcomed world leaders at Bharat Mandapam, against the backdrop of the iconic Ramanathaswamy Temple in Rameswaram, Tamil Nadu.

The two-day grand event brought together eleven Member nations and ten partner countries. During the high- level event, leaders of the BRICS member countries are expected to discuss key issues, including global governance, multilateralism, trade and investment, technology, food and energy security, healthcare, disaster resilience, and critical supply chains. The Summit is being held under India’s 2026 BRICS chairship, with the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability”.

Several key world leaders are participating in the high-profile summit, including Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. The BRICS Summit is bringing together 11 major emerging and developing economies, including Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, India, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, and the UAE. The partner countries are Belarus, Bolivia, Kazakhstan, Cuba, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, Uzbekistan and Vietnam are also participating in the summit.

passages.title: India at Commonwealth Games 2026
passages.text:
The Indian contingent for the Asian Games 2026  received a grand send-off in New Delhi yesterday in the presence of Youth Affairs and Sports Minister Dr. Mansukh Mandaviya. Dr. Mandaviya, along with Indian Olympic Association President P T Usha, Sports Secretary Hari Ranjan Rao, and Chef de Mission Sahdev Yadav, unveiled the official jersey of the Indian contingent in the presence of athletes and support staff.

Addressing the gathering, Dr. Mandaviya urged Indian athletes to turn pressure into performance, view opponents as opportunities and transform those opportunities into achievements. Highlighting Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s vision for Indian sports, he said the Government has created new pathways for athletes to compete and excel at the global level.

Dr Mandaviya also highlighted the growing depth of Indian sport and the emergence of young talent. He said that out of the 503-member contingent, more than three hundred athletes are first-time participants at the Asian Games. Applauding India’s performance at the Commonwealth Games 2026 in Glasgow, the Union Minister said at the last Commonwealth Games, India won 13 gold medals and this time the tally has improved by more than 35 per cent. He said the target is to establish India firmly on the world sporting stage by 2036, when the country aims to host the Olympic Games. He added that this ten-year plan includes an allocation of more than 36 thousand crore rupees for improving sports infrastructure.

passages.title: Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026
passages.text:
The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026, proposes tighter rules for Indian organisations that receive foreign funds. The Bill seeks to change rules on registration, renewal and the handling of foreign- funded assets. It also proposes changes relating to organisations that receive foreign funds through the prior- permission route, the responsibilities of key functionaries and investigations into FCRA violations.

The Centre says the changes are meant to address gaps that have emerged in the administration of the existing law, improve transparency and ensure that foreign funds are used only for permitted purposes. But critics are concerned. Christian organisations, NGOs and minority groups fear that the new rules could increase paperwork and administrative demands. They also worry that officials may get wider powers to act against organisations and that mistakes or delays in compliance could have serious consequences for legitimate charitable and religious work.

The Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha on March 25, 2026, and referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) on August 12 for examination. It is still under consideration. Separately, the revised FCRA Rules were notified on June 22 and are already in force. The Rules specify permitted purposes and States/Union Territories of operation, introduce new disclosure requirements and prescribe conditions for demonstrating reasonable activity.

Extracted with edits and revisions from https://www.newindianexpress.com/explainers/2026/Aug/24/fcra-bill- 2026-what-does-it-change-and-what-are-the-concerns

passages.title: Parliament Passes Bill to Rename Kerala as Keralam
passages.text:
The Parliament has passed the Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill, 2026, with the Rajya Sabha approving it today. The Lok Sabha had passed the legislation yesterday. The Bill seeks to change the name of the state of Kerala to Keralam in the First Schedule of the Constitution.

Replying to a debate on the Bill, Minister of State for Home Nityanand Rai said the Kerala Legislative Assembly had passed a resolution in 2024, requesting the Centre to change the name of the State from Kerala to Keralam. He said the request in this regard was made because the name of the State in Malayalam is Keralam, while in the Constitution, it is written as Kerala. The Minister said that the Union Cabinet in February this year approved the proposal to change the name of the state to Keralam and to introduce the necessary legislation for amendment in this regard. He said the Union Government brought the Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill, 2026 in the Parliament to honour the State’s request. Earlier, participating in the discussion, Tarun Chugh of BJP said the motto of this bill is to change the name from Kerala to Keralam and to erase the signs of slavery and restore the glory.

Jyoti Waghmare of Shiv Sena said the name is the first identity of any person or place and renaming Kerala to Keralam is a way to honour the Malayalam language. Participating in the discussion, Union Minister Suresh Gopi said, passage of the Bill is a celebratory moment for over four crore Malayalis around the globe. He alleged that in the presence of Congress and CPI (M) Members, the Bill was not allowed to be discussed in the Lok Sabha.

passages.title: Vande Mataram Bill passed
passages.text:
Parliament has passed the Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026. Minister of State for Home Nityanand Rai  moved the bill to further amend the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971. The legislation seeks to give Vande Mataram the same statutory protection as the national anthem, Jana Gana Mana. These offences are punishable with imprisonment up to three years, a fine, or both.

Earlier, replying to the discussion on the Bill, Minister of State for Home Nityanand Rai said, the bill is not merely a legislative amendment, but it represents India’s cultural heritage, national identity, and the ideals of the country’s freedom struggle. He said, in 1971, through the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, provisions were made to ensure respect for the National Anthem. The Minister said Vande Mataram is not just a song, but it is the voice of the nation’s soul. Mr Rai added the Vande Mataram song has been a source of inspiration for the country’s freedom fighters. He said, on 15th August 1947, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel had asked Pandit Omkarnath Thakur to render the complete Vande Mataram on All India Radio at 6:30 in the morning, marking the beginning of the first Independence Day. The Minister said that through this bill, the ideals of unity, respect, and the immortal legacy of the nation’s freedom struggle will be further strengthened.

Participating in the discussion, K Kanimozhi of DMK opposed the legislation, claiming that the Bill divides people across the country. Supporting the bill, Sambit Patra of BJP said the legislation is very important. He said the central government is observing a year-long national commemoration for the 150th anniversary of the national song Vande Mataram from November last year. He said that through the bill, the Narendra Modi Government is giving legal protection to the National Song.

Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 in Force The Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) [VB-G RAM G] Act, 2025 came into force across rural India on Wednesday, marking a major overhaul of the country’s rural employment framework by increasing the statutory employment guarantee from 100 days to 125 days for every eligible rural household.

The legislation aims to strengthen livelihood security, create durable rural assets and accelerate the vision of Viksit Bharat @2047 through enhanced employment opportunities and sustainable rural development.

Describing the rollout as a “historic and unprecedented” moment, Union Minister for Rural Development and Agriculture & Farmers’ Welfare Shivraj Singh Chouhan said the new law represents a significant step towards ensuring dignity, self-respect and secure livelihoods for millions of rural workers.

In a post on X, Chouhan said, “Today is a historic and unprecedented day. Under the leadership of Honorable Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi Ji, the Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Employment and Livelihood Mission (Rural) has been implemented across the country today. This is not just an act, but a new chapter of dignity, self- respect, and secure livelihood for crores of our rural worker brothers and sisters. Now, rural households will get a statutory right to 125 days of employment instead of 100.” “I am fully confident that this initiative will create new livelihood opportunities in villages, accelerate the creation of durable assets, empower women (Matrushakti), and give a new momentum to the building of a self-reliant rural India,” he added.

passages.title: India to Assume Vice-Presidency of FATF for 1st Time
passages.text:
India has been chosen for the incoming vice presidency of the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), the global money laundering and terror financing watchdog. Vivek Aggarwal, a 1994-batch officer of the Indian Administrative Service (Madhya Pradesh cadre) and presently Secretary, Ministry of Culture, has been elected and appointed as the vice president of FATF from July 2026 to June 2027. This is the first time India will have a leadership position at the global body. The vice presidency for India also strengthens India’s chances for assuming the presidency role when the next switchover happens at the FATF after two years, officials said.

The FATF has 40 members, and over 200 jurisdictions have committed to the FATF recommendations through the FATF-style regional bodies. The FATF Presidency runs on a two-year term, and the vice-president assists the president in carrying out the organisation’s mandate. The Ministry of Finance in a statement released late Friday said that this decision marks a “landmark recognition” of India’s growing leadership in the global fight against money laundering and terrorist financing.

“The vice-president of the FATF is elected by the FATF Plenary from among its members and assists the president in steering the organisation’s work. The appointment places an Indian official at the apex of the global standard-setting body for anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing. India’s elevation to the vice- presidency reflects the credibility and trust the country has earned within the FATF Global Network of more than 200 jurisdictions,” the ministry said.

Extracted with edits and revisions https://indianexpress.com/article/business/india-fatf-vice-presidency-vivek- aggarwal-appointed-10748670/

passages.title: World Bank Income Classification: India Remains Lower-Middle-Income
passages.text:
In the World Bank’s classification of global economies, five countries moved from lower-middle to upper- middle income category this year. The World Bank’s classification is updated based on gross national income (GNI) per capita estimates from the previous calendar year.

India’s economy grew at 7.8% in the April-June quarter of 2026-27. But the country’s per capita income stood around US$ 2671 in the FY 2024-25. Where does India stand in the World Bank’s latest classification of global economies? The World Development Report 2024: The Middle-Income Trap identified a total of 108 countries, including India, facing challenges in moving away from the trap. Compared with the US, the report noted, these countries are trapped at modest income levels.

Using estimates based on the Solow-Swan model of growth, the report projects that these countries are likely to experience a significant slowdown between 2024 and 2100 if the drivers of growth remain as per their current and historic trends. The drivers of growth in this model are investment in human capital, total factor productivity, labour force participation, and the share of economic output accrued to public and private investment.

Extracted with edits and revisions from https://indianexpress.com/article/upsc-current-affairs/upsc-essentials/is- innovation-the-only-way-out-of-the-middle-income-trap-10870393/

passages.title: Centre Proposes Special Article 371 Framework for Ladakh
passages.text:
The Ladakh administration said Thursday that the new governance arrangement for the Union Territory will neither be statehood nor a UT with a legislature but a special constitutional amendment that will need the approval of Parliament.

A day after the meeting between representatives from Ladakh and officials of the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) in New Delhi, Ladakh Chief Secretary Ashish Kundra said that the agreement reached with the leadership here “is that a sui generis model, which does not exist anywhere in the country, will be crafted for Ladakh, where a legislative body will be created”.

“Ladakh was never a State. It was part of J&K, and later it became a UT. The aspiration of the people is to have legislative, executive, and financial powers. An agreement has been reached with the leadership here: a sui generis model, which does not exist anywhere in the country, will be crafted for Ladakh, where a legislative body will be created,” he said.

He added: “It is not going to be Statehood for sure or a UT with legislature, but it is some other body which will have these powers; the nomenclature of it is yet to be finalised, that is why discussions are on.” Kundra said that the framework proposed for Ladakh is a constitutional amendment and not the enactment of an “ordinary law”. For this, he said, a two-thirds majority is needed “and that requires political consensus across parties.” After this, he added, a detailed regulation to implement this decision will be needed. “These things have been transparently shared with the leadership yesterday.”

passages.title: The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement
passages.text:
The Mecca Agreement can become the deterrent core of a layered security architecture stretching from the Eastern Mediterranean to South Asia—one that restrains Israeli escalation, leaves room for negotiated security with Iran, and turns political solidarity into institutional practice of regional peace without reproducing another closed bloc.

The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement should be read first as an idea, and only then as a military pact. Signed by Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan on 7 August 2026, it declares that an armed attack against one will be regarded as an attack against all and frames the arrangement as defensive collective deterrence. (1) Three weeks later, the three states moved from declaration to organisation: their foreign and defence ministers and military chiefs met in Istanbul, agreed to establish a permanent secretariat in Saudi Arabia, and committed themselves to joint defence-industry cooperation, technology development and production. (2) The movement from declaration to organisation is therefore already visible; the harder transition is from organisation to durable institutional practice.

The timing is not accidental. The genocide in Gaza has been followed by Israeli operations across Lebanon, Syria, Yemen and Iran, while the latest India-Pakistan confrontation again showed that security crises do not respect neat regional boxes. “Middle East” remains a useful shorthand, but Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan connect the Mediterranean, Gulf, Red Sea, Indian Ocean and South Asia, which has a potential to redefine the “region”.

passages.title: Money Bill Route to Increase Supreme Court Judges’ Strength
passages.text:
The Rajya Sabha Wednesday passed the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026, which seeks to increase the sanctioned strength of Supreme Court judges from 34 to 38 including the Chief Justice of India.

The Bill, which cleared Lok Sabha Monday, was passed as a money Bill, a route it had also taken in 2019 when the Supre-me Court strength was raised to 34. In 2018, a key dissenting opinion in a Supreme Court ruling had described this route as a “fraud on the Constitution.”

The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill cites the expenditure involved in creating four additional posts of judges, along with staff, residences and security.

“This will increase the expenditure on account of pay and allowances on creation of four additional posts of Judges in the Supreme Court along with required staff. The Judges will also be entitled to the use of a rent-free official residence. Each Judge will have to be provided with personal staff at residence and office. Expenditure would also be incurred in connection with the deployment of security for Judges. ⁠The estimated recurring expenditure on salaries of four Judges and their staff, conveyance and other miscellaneous expenses would be rupees 10,56,81,648 per annum and non-recurring expenditure towards car and furnishing of official residence and other miscellaneous expenses will be approximately rupees 3,47,36,000. Thus, the total expenditure on creation of additional four posts of Judges in the Supreme Court of India will be of rupees 14,04,17,648 approximately,” the Bill stated.

The ancient Buddhist site of Sarnath has been inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Welcoming the inscription of Uttar Pradesh’s Sarnath on the UNESCO World Heritage List, Prime Minister Narendra Modi described it as a proud moment for every Indian.

In a social media post, PM Modi said that Sarnath has a close association with Lord Buddha, whose timeless message of wisdom, compassion, and harmony continues to inspire the world. He added that the recognition celebrates India’s profound civilisational and spiritual heritage. The Prime Minister said that the inscription would inspire more people from across the world to visit Sarnath and connect with the ideals of Lord Buddha.

Culture and Tourism Minister Gajendra Singh Shekhawat described the inscription as a defining moment for India’s cultural heritage. In a social media post, Mr Shekhawat said that Sarnath is a timeless beacon of peace, wisdom, and compassion. He said that it reflects the profound spiritual and philosophical contributions of Indian civilisation to humanity. Mr Shekhawat added that the inscription reaffirms the nation’s enduring role as a cradle of ideas that continue to inspire the world across generations.

passages.title: 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit
passages.text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday participated in the 26th Meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) in Bishkek, calling for stronger cooperation on security, connectivity and development while urging member countries to take committed action against terrorism.

The summit, held from August 31 to September 1 in the Kyrgyz Republic, coincides with the 25th anniversary of the SCO. Leaders reviewed the organisation’s progress and discussed ways to strengthen its role in promoting peace, security, stability and prosperity in the region. In his address, PM Modi thanked Kyrgyz President Sadyr Zhaparov for his warmth and hospitality and said the SCO’s 25th anniversary provided an opportunity to prepare a roadmap for the next 25 years, building on the organisation’s tradition of dialogue and cooperation.

Recalling India’s vision presented at the previous summit, the Prime Minister said the grouping should now work towards achieving concrete outcomes under the three pillars of Security, Connectivity and Opportunity. On security, PM Modi reiterated India’s position that conflicts cannot be resolved through military means and that dialogue and diplomacy are the only way forward. He described terrorism as a grave threat to humanity and called for determined efforts to dismantle the entire terror ecosystem.

passages.title: FIFA World Cup 2026
passages.text:
Spain won the 2026 FIFA World Cup, beating Argentina 1-0 in extra time in a final that closed a tournament defined as much by its politics as its football. Ferran Torres, on as a substitute, scored the winner in the 106th minute at the New York/New Jersey Stadium in East Rutherford, converting a pass from fellow substitute Nico Williams after Argentina had been reduced to 10 men through Enzo Fernández’s second yellow card. It was Spain’s second World Cup title, 16 years after its first.

Spain’s midfielder Rodri won the Golden Ball as the tournament’s outstanding player. Kylian Mbappé took the Golden Boot with 10 goals, two clear of Lionel Messi, and became the first player to win the award twice. Mbappé also finished with 22 career World Cup goals against Messi’s 21, taking the all-time scoring record; he later said he would have traded it for a place in the final. US President Donald Trump, who co-hosted the tournament with Canada and Mexico, presented the trophy alongside FIFA president Gianni Infantino. The half- time break of the final match featured performances of Madonna, Justin Bieber, Shakira, and BTS.

The 2026 edition—the first with 48 teams and 104 matches—drew 68,10,996 spectators across its stadiums, a record for the tournament and well above the previous mark of roughly 3.6 million, set at the 1994 World Cup in the US. FIFA has said the tournament will generate close to $9 billion in revenue for 2026 alone, part of a four-year commercial cycle in which its total income is expected to approach $13 billion; figures reported by FIFA and financial analysts vary somewhat depending on what is counted within the cycle.

passages.title: The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2026
passages.text: The closing days of the Monsoon Session this August saw Parliament clear the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 — passed by both Houses in mid-August — which has since become law with the President's assent. The parent statute has governed mines for nearly seven decades, but the provocation lay elsewhere: a 2024 Constitution Bench verdict holding that royalty is not really a tax, and recognising the power of State legislatures to tax mineral rights. Emboldened, some States levied cesses touching a fifth of a mineral's value, atop the fourteen-odd taxes, charges and fees miners already shoulder. Industry warned that every pithead rupee travels through steel, cement and electricity into the price of an ordinary family's home — even as mineral imports stood at ₹10.12 lakh crore in 2025-26. The Amendment rewrites this fiscal grammar. For the first time, the Union's reach extends expressly to the land that holds minerals, not merely to mines alone. A newly-inserted provision forbids State Governments from taxing mineral rights or mineral-bearing lands — by whatever name called — save under conditions and restrictions the Centre will prescribe through rules. Retrospective peace follows: demands raised but never recovered stand extinguished, while money already in State coffers stays put. The Centre's assurance is that nearly nine-tenths of the sector's revenues shall continue to accrue to States, whose writ over sand, gravel and some fifty minor minerals remains untouched, as do District Mineral Foundation collections under the PMKKKY. Beyond taxation, the country's exploration trust, hitherto confined to prospecting support, will now finance mine development as well, and be rechristened to match this wider role. Blocks with deep-seated deposits may expand once — by a tenth of a mining lease or three-tenths of a composite licence — and an authority shall register and regulate mineral exchanges.

passages.title: Vikram-1 — India's First Private Orbital Rocket (Skyroot Aerospace)
passages.text: History does not always arrive with noise; sometimes it lifts off past noon from a barrier island on the Coromandel coast. On the eighteenth of July, a seven-storey, all-carbon-composite rocket rose from the First Launch Pad of the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, and within a quarter of an hour had slipped its payloads into an orbit some 450 kilometres up. Mission Aagaman, its builders declared, had met every objective. The architect of this triumph is a Hyderabad startup founded eight years ago by two engineers who once drew ISRO salaries, born of the 2020 reforms that unlocked the space sector for private enterprise; earlier this year it crossed the billion-dollar valuation mark, a first for any Indian spacetech firm. The vehicle pairs solid muscle with additive brains: three stages of solid propellant, capped by a liquid orbital- adjustment module whose 3D-printed engine coaxed the payloads into their precise slots — technologies flown for the first time in India. The manifest was suitably mixed: a German customer's satellite, an orbital bodyguard in the form of a robotic arm designed to snare debris, an Indian Earth-observation camera, and a diamond-themed artwork headed for weightlessness. The date carried a quiet symmetry: exactly forty-six years earlier, from the same coast, India's first home-grown satellite launcher had risen, dragging the nation into an elite club. Now private enterprise has repeated the rite, admitting India — behind superpowers — into a still more exclusive club: countries whose companies can hurl satellites into orbit themselves. Regulator, promoter and landlord watched together: the national space-promotion centre authorised the flight, the national space agency's range hosted it. Its suborbital forerunner had already kissed space from this shore; a heavier sibling now sits on the drawing board for next year.

passages.title: The "Creamy Layer" Concept in SC/ST Reservations
passages.text: The reservation debate travels in circles, but every few decades the circle widens. The doctrine of the "creamy layer" was born in the early nineties, when a nine-judge bench upheld job and college quotas for the Other Backward Classes and, in the same breath, ruled that the socially and economically advanced among them must be skimmed off the beneficiaries' list. For three decades that sieve filtered only OBC lists; the Scheduled Castes and Tribes stood apart, treated since a 2004 pronouncement as single, indivisible classes whose internal fortunes only Parliament could re-sort. That changed on the first of August two years ago, when a bench of seven judges declared — six voices strong — that States may slice the SC and ST quotas internally, prioritising the most backward among the backward, provided the carve-up rests on quantifiable, demonstrable data and not political whimsy. No sub-caste may swallow the whole pie; the Presidential lists themselves remain untouched. But it was a rider that set Delhi abuzz: one judge, himself from the community, asked whether a child in an elite metropolitan school and an elite college could honestly be bracketed with a child in a remote village school — and answered that the prosperous must step aside. Another pressed that benefits should end with the first generation to rise. The lone dissenter warned that State legislatures were creeping onto Parliament's turf over the designated lists, which only the Centre could define. Two monsoons later, the argument has sharpened again. Before a fresh larger bench weighing implementation, the Union has insisted that prosperity does not launder away the stigma of caste — that, whatever the judges mused, no "creamy layer" can legally be carved out of these communities. Meanwhile, one southern State has already written internal quotas into its statute book, and others are busy counting their castes.

passages.title: India and the Bid for Permanent UNSC Membership
passages.text: The waiting room of the United Nations has some famously patient applicants. Its newest campaign, launched this monsoon, canvasses one more elected stint before the decade turns. At a spring session of the reform talks this year, India drew its line in the sand: any new permanent chairs arriving without the full privileges of the old five would merely worsen the imbalance, institutionalising a graded club it refuses to join. Yet it also played a card of flexibility — endorsing, with three fellow aspirants, a compromise under which newcomers would observe a long probation before touching the most coveted prerogative, their restraint to be weighed at a promised review. The arithmetic against reform is brutal. The Charter's amendment machinery, never once used to expand permanence, hands every incumbent a blocking card; and one incumbent in particular is widely seen in New Delhi as quietly throttling India's bid, entangling it with a Himalayan frontier dispute. Meanwhile the so-called "coffee club" — Italy chief among its vocalists — argues that more veto-wielders would only paralyse the Council further. India's counter leans on history. The Council's solitary enlargement, six decades ago, padded only the elected benches, skewing the permanent-to-elected ratio ever since; an enlargement that tweaks everything except permanence, its envoy argues, would stretch the imbalance further. The continent-wide bloc nursing its own demand — two permanent chairs for a region shut out of 1945's spoils — frowns at the compromise, seeing pauper's permanence where the aspirants see pragmatism. By midsummer, at the stocktake of a future-facing compact adopted by world leaders two Septembers ago, New Delhi dismissed the talking shop as an eternity of prepared statements with action points frozen on paper. An eighty-year-old architecture designed for the 1940s, it warned, cannot police the 2020s. India, fresh off its eighth elected stint and eyeing the decade ahead, no longer intends to ask politely. Alongside its longer-term demand for permanent representation, India has also begun its campaign for another elected term on the Council for 2028–29, presenting the bid as part of its wider engagement with multilateral institutions.”

passages.title: India's Cultural Diplomacy — Soft Power through Global Engagement
passages.text: On a December evening, within the ramparts of a Mughal-era citadel on the Yamuna, the world formally adopted India's festival of lights as a jewel of humanity's living heritage — the first time the safeguarding committee met on Indian soil. Among sixty-odd nominations tabled that week, it was arguably the most luminous, and when the gavel fell, chants of celebration rang through the venue's ancient walls. For New Delhi, the moment was less an end than an exhibit: soft power in its natural habitat. Soft power — influence that seduces rather than compels, as a Harvard professor framed it in the nineties — India exercises through what it simply lives. A summer-solstice morning now bends plazas from Times Square to the Seine into yoga mats; a humble ancient grain once secured a whole calendar year from the world body; a WHO outpost for traditional medicine stands on Gujarat's coast; relics of the Buddha draw millions in Hanoi and Elista; a revived Nalanda enrols the world again; last year, a dozen sentinel forts — from Sahyadri crags to a lone southern outpost — marched into the heritage list at Paris; and several more tongues, Pali and Prakrit among them, now wear classical ribbons. None of this is accident. A cultural council founded in 1950 wires out teachers, troupes and scholarships across scores of countries; a six-decade-old training programme schoolmasters the Global South's bureaucracies; diaspora jamborees turn migration into memory. Coercion, the old argument goes, buys obedience; culture rents hearts. India's lease on that real estate, evidently, runs long.

passages.text: The approaching conclusion of the existing Ganga water-sharing arrangement has reopened a complex debate involving India, Bangladesh and Indian States situated along the river system. What began principally as a bilateral question of allocating dry-season river flows has increasingly become intertwined with concerns about federalism, climate change, sedimentation, ecological resilience and future water demand. Bihar has emerged as a significant domestic stakeholder in the debate. Its political leadership has argued that any future arrangement must take account of the State’s drinking-water, irrigation and industrial requirements, as well as problems associated with floods and sediment accumulation. Several Indian States have also sought greater consultation because domestic water requirements and river-management concerns are closely connected with the bilateral negotiations. This has made negotiations not merely an exercise in foreign policy but also one of internal federal consultation. Bangladesh, as the downstream country, has historically emphasised adequate dry-season availability and the environmental consequences of reduced flows. Meanwhile, changing rainfall patterns, upstream withdrawals and wider climatic pressures have made historical flow assumptions increasingly uncertain. Experts have therefore argued that a future agreement may need to go beyond a narrow allocation formula and incorporate ecological protection, data-sharing, flood forecasting, sediment management and stronger institutional cooperation. The controversy demonstrates how transboundary rivers create interdependence rather than a simple contest between upstream and downstream States. An enduring framework will therefore require India and Bangladesh to reconcile diplomatic obligations with domestic concerns while adapting river governance to ecological and hydrological conditions that have changed significantly since the existing arrangement was negotiated. Adapted from The Indian Express coverage and analysis of the Ganga Water-Sharing Treaty debate, July– September 2026.

passages.title: Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026
passages.text:
Parliament’s decision in 2026 to expand the sanctioned judicial strength of the Supreme Court reopened a wider debate about institutional capacity, case pendency and the constitutional role of the country’s highest court. The government argued that additional judicial capacity could help the Court manage its growing docket and enable larger Benches to sit more regularly without excessively disrupting ordinary appellate work. The Supreme Court performs several functions simultaneously. It decides constitutional questions while also hearing civil and criminal appeals, writ petitions, special leave petitions and other matters. Constitution Benches

require several judges to sit together, temporarily reducing the number available for smaller Benches. Consequently, increasing judicial strength may give the Chief Justice greater flexibility in constituting different Bench combinations. However, commentators have cautioned that simply increasing sanctioned posts does not automatically reduce pendency; vacancies, case-management practices, institutional procedures and the volume of new litigation also matter. The legislative route chosen for the measure generated a separate constitutional debate. Because creating additional judicial posts involves expenditure from public funds, the legislation was processed through a category of Bill for which the two Houses of Parliament exercise different powers. Critics questioned whether this classification was appropriate, linking the controversy to a broader unresolved debate over the constitutional boundaries of such legislation. The episode therefore raises two distinct questions: whether increasing judicial capacity can meaningfully improve the functioning of the Supreme Court, and whether legislation affecting institutional expenditure should be enacted through a procedure that gives the Upper House a more limited role. Adapted from The Indian Express and Government of India coverage of the Supreme Court judge-strength legislation, 2026.

passages.title: Indian Standard Time
passages.text:
As banking, telecommunications, power grids, transport networks and digital governance become increasingly dependent on precise timestamps, even small inconsistencies between clocks can create operational and security problems. In 2026, the Union government introduced a new regulatory framework intended to make the country's official time a uniform and traceable reference for government institutions, businesses and critical infrastructure. The initiative goes beyond displaying the same time on clocks. Modern digital systems obtain timing signals from servers, satellite-navigation networks and other technological sources. If different systems rely on unrelated or externally controlled references, discrepancies may affect financial transactions, telecommunications, network

logs and infrastructure coordination. Manipulation of timing signals through techniques such as spoofing or jamming can also create cybersecurity risks. The new framework therefore emphasises traceability, meaning that the time used by an organisation should be capable of being linked through recognised standards to India's national time reference. Critical systems are also expected to incorporate redundancy so that failure or manipulation of one timing source does not disrupt essential services. India is simultaneously expanding domestic infrastructure for secure dissemination of precise time, including satellite-based and laboratory-linked mechanisms. The reform reflects a broader shift in legal metrology. Traditionally associated with ensuring the accuracy of measurements used in commerce, metrology increasingly intersects with digital governance, cybersecurity and critical infrastructure. A legally recognised national time reference can therefore serve not merely as a convention for setting clocks, but as an essential standard for reliable electronic records, transactions and communication systems. Adapted from PIB and The Indian Express coverage of the Legal Metrology (Indian Standard Time) Rules, 2026.

passages.title: India Australia Summit
passages.text:
India and Australia have steadily transformed their relationship from one centred largely on trade and education into a wider strategic partnership encompassing security, technology, energy and regional cooperation. Their latest annual summit reflected this evolution, with both sides seeking greater coordination in an Indo-Pacific increasingly shaped by supply-chain vulnerabilities, maritime security concerns and competition over critical technologies. Defence cooperation featured prominently. The two countries agreed to deepen operational coordination, information-sharing, military exchanges and defence-industrial collaboration. Maritime security received particular attention because both nations view secure sea lanes and adherence to international law as essential to regional stability. Cooperation now extends beyond bilateral exercises to capacity-building and coordination through regional institutions. Economic security formed another major pillar. The leaders discussed expanding bilateral trade, reducing non- tariff barriers and developing resilient supply chains for critical minerals and energy resources. Technology

cooperation was broadened to include cybersecurity, emerging technologies and trusted supply networks. Clean energy, renewable power and civil nuclear cooperation were also identified as important elements of long-term energy security. Education, skills, research and mobility continued to support strong people-to-people ties. The summit also highlighted growing cooperation in space, including support for India's human spaceflight programme, alongside new initiatives in sports and vocational training. The expanding agenda illustrates how India-Australia relations increasingly combine economic opportunity with strategic convergence. Their cooperation now operates bilaterally as well as through regional platforms, with both countries emphasising an open, stable and rules-based Indo-Pacific. Adapted from PIB and The Indian Express coverage of the 2026 India–Australia Annual Summit.

passages.title: Greenland Issue & Arctic Governance
passages.text:
Greenland returned to the centre of international attention in 2026 as its geographical position, critical-mineral potential and importance to North Atlantic affairs generated renewed strategic interest. In September, the governments of the United States, Denmark and Greenland signed an agreement aimed at strengthening security cooperation in the Arctic and North Atlantic. The arrangement supplements an earlier defence framework and also addresses Greenlandic interests, sovereignty and self-determination. The development has also renewed discussion about the roles played by NATO, the Arctic Council and other mechanisms of regional cooperation. These institutions operate under different mandates and legal foundations, making Arctic governance an important subject in contemporary international relations. Climate change has added another dimension. Declining sea ice may affect shipping patterns, resource accessibility and scientific activity, while questions involving maritime boundaries and continental-shelf claims

bring the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) into the debate. Comparisons with the legal arrangements governing Antarctica have consequently received greater attention. India also has a growing scientific interest in the region. Its Arctic research programme includes the Himadri research station, through which Indian researchers undertake studies relating to climate, atmosphere, glaciers and polar processes. The Greenland issue therefore brings together strategic competition, international law, scientific research, climate change and the evolving geopolitical importance of the polar regions.

passages.title: From Kerala to Keralam
passages.text: In 2026, the Union government moved forward with a long-pending proposal concerning the official name of one of India’s southern States. The initiative followed a resolution adopted by the State legislature and revived discussion on how linguistic identity, federal consultation and constitutional procedure interact when the name of a State is altered. The proposal was subsequently considered by the Union Cabinet and taken through the parliamentary process. Press Information Bureau The development was rooted in a broader historical context. The State had been reorganised in the 1950s as part of the restructuring of India’s internal boundaries largely on linguistic lines. Over the decades, questions of language and regional identity continued to influence demands relating to the names of States, cities and other geographical entities. Unlike an ordinary administrative change, however, altering the official name of a State involves a constitutionally prescribed process in which both Union institutions and the concerned State legislature have defined roles. The Constitution gives Parliament significant authority over the formation of States and changes relating to their areas, boundaries and names. At the same time, the federal structure requires consultation with the legislature of the affected State before Parliament proceeds with such legislation. The State’s opinion forms part of this process, although the Constitution does not place the final legislative decision solely in its hands. The 2026 development therefore illustrates an important feature of Indian federalism: changes to the political map or constitutional identity of a State may originate from regional aspirations, but their formal recognition requires action through national constitutional institutions. The episode also highlights how India’s constitutional framework accommodates territorial and nomenclatural changes without necessarily invoking the procedure used for every formal constitutional amendment.

passages.title: India’s Push Towards Ethanol Blending and Cleaner Mobility
passages.text: India’s transport-fuel policy has increasingly incorporated biofuels as part of a wider effort to diversify the country’s energy mix. Among the measures receiving sustained policy attention is the blending of ethanol with conventional petrol. The initiative has expanded progressively over the years, supported by changes in production capacity, fuel-distribution infrastructure and automobile standards. The transition involves several sectors simultaneously. Ethanol production depends on the availability of suitable domestic raw materials and sufficient processing capacity, while fuel suppliers must maintain prescribed quality and blending standards. At the same time, the automobile industry must ensure that vehicles placed on the market can operate efficiently with fuels containing a higher proportion of ethanol. These technical requirements have made coordination between government agencies, fuel companies, vehicle manufacturers and research institutions increasingly important. The policy also has wider economic implications. India remains heavily dependent on imported crude petroleum, making international price movements and supply disruptions important considerations in domestic energy planning. Greater use of alternative fuels is therefore viewed as one element of a broader strategy to improve resilience in the transport-energy sector. Parallel initiatives have also encouraged the development of newer generations of biofuels using technologies capable of converting different forms of biomass into usable energy products. These efforts seek to complement conventional fuel-blending programmes by encouraging innovation, investment and more efficient use of domestic resources. The expansion of ethanol-blended petrol thus reflects a broader transformation in India’s fuel policy, involving energy security, technological adaptation, domestic production and long-term changes in the transport sector. Its implementation continues to depend on coordination across multiple institutions and industries.

passages.title: India–U.S. Cooperation in Lunar and Deep-Space Exploration
passages.text: India and the United States have steadily expanded cooperation in outer space from satellite applications and Earth observation to human spaceflight, planetary science and long-term lunar exploration. In 2026, this partnership gained fresh momentum as both sides explored possibilities for India to participate in future American-led efforts aimed at establishing a sustained human presence on the Moon. The discussions formed part of an established bilateral dialogue dedicated to civil space cooperation. Officials reviewed ongoing projects and examined opportunities in lunar science, human spaceflight, planetary exploration, scientific data sharing and commercial space activities. The interaction reflected India's growing role in international space collaboration and the increasing technological depth of its own space programme. Recent cooperation between the two countries has already produced a major joint Earth-observation satellite designed to study changes in forests, glaciers, agriculture and the Earth's surface with high precision. Experience gained from such technically complex collaboration has been viewed as a useful foundation for undertaking more ambitious ventures in the future. Lunar cooperation is also linked to a wider international framework that promotes peaceful, transparent and responsible exploration of the Moon and other celestial bodies. India joined this framework earlier in the decade, signalling its willingness to participate in rule-based international cooperation in outer space. India's expanding role in such initiatives also reflects the evolution of its own space programme. What began with a development-oriented vision focused on communication, meteorology and national needs has gradually expanded to include lunar exploration, Mars missions, solar observation and preparations for human spaceflight. The principles laid down by India's early space pioneers continue to influence this approach even as the country takes on increasingly complex missions. The emerging partnership therefore combines India's indigenous capabilities with international cooperation and may shape its role in the next phase of lunar and deep-space exploration.

passages.title: 75 Years of India’s First Constitutional Amendment
passages.text: In 2026, India marked seventy-five years of its first amendment to the Constitution, an early intervention that continues to occupy an important place in debates on constitutional democracy. Adopted when the Constitution itself was barely a year and a half old, the amendment emerged from tensions between newly guaranteed fundamental rights and the social and economic policies being pursued by governments in the early years of the Republic. Several developments had brought these tensions into sharp focus. Courts were being called upon to examine restrictions imposed by the State, measures intended to benefit disadvantaged sections, and legislation designed to restructure agrarian relations. The Union government maintained that constitutional changes were necessary to ensure that elected governments retained sufficient space to pursue reform while operating within the framework of fundamental rights. The amendment consequently affected more than one field of constitutional governance. Its provisions had implications for freedom of expression, affirmative State action, economic regulation and land reform. Some of its innovations also sought to give specified legislation a degree of constitutional protection from fundamental- rights challenges. Its significance extended beyond the immediate policies of the 1950s. Soon after its enactment, its constitutional validity itself came before the Supreme Court, beginning a long judicial debate over Parliament’s power to amend the Constitution. In later decades, that debate would evolve considerably and become central to Indian constitutional law. [Adapted from the Statement of Objects and Reasons to the Constitution (First Amendment) Bill, 1951, and subsequent constitutional developments.]

passages.title: VB-G RAM G and the New Rural Employment Framework
passages.text: India’s rural employment architecture underwent a major transition in 2026 with the operationalisation of a new statutory framework aimed at combining wage employment with longer-term rural development. The new system retains the idea that eligible rural households may demand unskilled manual work, but seeks to connect such employment more closely with productive asset creation, livelihood security and infrastructure planning. The framework reflects a broader shift from viewing public employment primarily as short-term income support towards integrating it with village-level development. Greater emphasis has been placed on decentralised planning, convergence between government programmes, technology-enabled monitoring and the creation of assets capable of supporting agriculture, water security and resilience to extreme weather events. The new architecture also modifies the financial relationship between the Union and the States. Instead of following a uniform financing arrangement, the law provides differentiated cost-sharing patterns according to the category of State or Union Territory. State governments are also given responsibilities relating to implementation, unemployment support and identification of periods during which agricultural labour demand is particularly high. At the institutional level, Gram Panchayats and other local bodies continue to play an important role in translating the statutory guarantee into actual employment. The framework therefore operates at the intersection of several constitutional ideas: livelihood security, decentralised governance, cooperative federalism and the State’s responsibility to promote social and economic welfare. The reform has consequently become important not merely as a rural-development measure, but also for understanding the evolution of India's employment-guarantee policy and the constitutional architecture within which rural governance operates.

passages.title: G7 Summit 2026 and Emerging Global Priorities
passages.text:
The 52nd G7 Summit was held in Évian-les-Bains, France, in June 2026 under the French presidency. Besides the seven member countries, several partner nations, including India, Brazil, South Korea, and Kenya, participated as invited guests. The summit took place amid significant geopolitical and economic uncertainty, with discussions focusing on Ukraine, developments in West Asia, critical mineral supply chains, artificial intelligence governance, debt vulnerabilities in developing countries, and global economic imbalances.

A major theme of the summit was reducing excessive dependence on concentrated supply chains for critical minerals essential to clean energy technologies, semiconductors, and advanced manufacturing. Leaders also discussed the growing strategic significance of artificial intelligence and the need to balance innovation with accountability and safety. Ukraine remained a central agenda item, while concerns over maritime trade routes and energy security featured prominently in discussions concerning the Middle East.

India used the platform to highlight the concerns of the Global South and engaged in multiple bilateral meetings with G7 leaders. The summit also reflected broader debates regarding the future of global governance, as emerging economies continue to seek a greater voice in institutions originally designed in the post-Second World War era. India further expressed support for Canada becoming a Dialogue Partner of the Indian Ocean Rim Association (IORA) and welcomed the establishment of "Raisina Americas" to promote strategic dialogue and policy engagement across the Americas.

passages.title: Indus Water Treaty
passages.text:
Addressing concerns relating to cross-border terrorism and bilateral relations, the Government of India recently reiterated its position that the Indus Waters Treaty of 1960 would remain in abeyance until Pakistan takes credible and irreversible steps against terrorism. India also rejected the jurisdiction exercised by a Court of Arbitration constituted under the treaty framework regarding disputes linked to the Kishanganga and Ratle hydroelectric projects.

The Government maintained that the treaty provides a graded dispute-resolution mechanism involving the Permanent Indus Commission, a Neutral Expert and, in specified circumstances, a Court of Arbitration. India argued that simultaneous invocation of different mechanisms was inconsistent with the treaty architecture.

The Indus Waters Treaty, signed in 1960 with the assistance of the World Bank, allocates the waters of six rivers of the Indus basin between the two countries. The treaty has survived multiple wars and periods of diplomatic tension and is often cited as one of the most enduring international water-sharing arrangements.

The recent developments have revived discussions regarding transboundary water governance, hydroelectric development in Jammu and Kashmir, international arbitration, and the role of international institutions in managing river systems that cross sovereign borders.

passages.title: 50th anniversary of Sikkim
passages.text:
This year marks the 50th anniversary of Sikkim’s integration with India, commemorating the events of 1975 when Sikkim became the 22nd State of the Indian Union. Prior to its integration, Sikkim was ruled by the Chogyal dynasty and functioned as an Indian protectorate under a special treaty arrangement. Political developments during the early 1970s, including demands for democratic reforms and greater political representation, altered the relationship between the monarchy and elected institutions.

In 1975, the Sikkim Assembly adopted a resolution seeking the abolition of the institution of the Chogyal and closer constitutional integration with India. Subsequently, a referendum was conducted in which an overwhelming majority reportedly supported the proposal. Parliament enacted the Constitution Amendment Act, 1975, granting Sikkim full statehood. The amendment also inserted Article 371F, providing special constitutional provisions for the state.

Sikkim occupies a strategically important position in the eastern Himalayas, sharing borders with Nepal, Bhutan, and China. The state is also associated with significant geographical features such as Kanchenjunga, India’s highest mountain peak. The anniversary has renewed discussions on federalism, constitutional integration, border security, and the unique historical processes through which different regions became part of the Indian Union.

passages.title: India–Nepal Relations: New Momentum Amid Old Challenges
passages.text: Prime Minister of India and the Prime Minister of Nepal recently held bilateral talks in New Delhi focusing on economic cooperation, connectivity, energy security and regional stability. Both leaders reviewed progress under various infrastructure projects and emphasized the importance of people-to-people ties. They also discussed avenues for strengthening cooperation in digital payments, cross-border transport and renewable energy. The leaders reiterated their commitment to maintaining close coordination in regional and multilateral forums and agreed to enhance institutional mechanisms for addressing outstanding issues. The visit comes amid evolving geopolitical dynamics in the Himalayan region and renewed emphasis on connectivity and economic integration across South Asia. Both sides expressed confidence that stronger cooperation would contribute to prosperity, stability and sustainable development in the region.

passages.title: Base Year of Wholesale Price Index Revised
passages.text:
India recently initiated a major reform in its system of measuring price movements in the economy. The exercise forms part of a broader effort to modernize official statistics and align domestic practices with evolving international standards. Policymakers have increasingly emphasized the need for inflation indicators that capture production-stage price changes more accurately, particularly in an economy witnessing rapid diversification of manufacturing, services, and energy sectors.

The reform comes at a time when governments across the world are re-evaluating traditional measures of inflation to better understand how rising costs faced by producers eventually influence prices paid by consumers. Such measures are important not only for macroeconomic policy but also for infrastructure contracts, industrial planning, and assessment of economic competitiveness. Economists argue that modern inflation tracking should reflect changes in technology, production structures, and the growing role of services in national output.

The revised framework also seeks to improve the treatment of emerging industries and energy sources while incorporating more sophisticated statistical techniques. International organizations have repeatedly encouraged countries to strengthen producer-level price indicators as a complement to consumer inflation measures. Such indicators are often used to analyse cost pressures within supply chains and assess whether inflationary shocks are temporary or likely to persist.

The initiative reflects a broader trend in economic governance where statistical systems are periodically updated to remain representative of contemporary economic realities. Similar revisions have been undertaken by many countries as part of efforts to improve evidence-based policymaking and economic forecasting.
